speaker: Devi
title: Devi Opens the Tantra Inquiry
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरि तन्त्रम्
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
श्रुतं देि मया सिं रुद्रयामलसम्भवम् ।
विकभेदमशेषेण सारात्सारविभागश् ॥ १ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairi tantram
vijñānabhairava tantram
श्रुतं देवी मया सर्वं रुद्रयामलसम्भवम् |
vikalpabhedam aśeṣeṇa sārāt sāravibhāgaśaḥ || 1 ||
translation: I have heard, O Goddess, all of the Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra, arising from the Rudrayāmala, with the distinctions of विकल्प (vikalpa) fully divided, section by section from essence to essence.
intent_summary: Devi introduces the sacred teaching and frames it as a revelation to be clarified and distilled.
beginner_explanation: This verse sets the scene: the Goddess says she has heard the teaching and wants its essence. It is like asking for the main point after receiving a long and complex lesson. The focus is on separating what is essential from what is secondary.
scholar_explanation: This opening establishes the tantra as a transmission from the Rudrayāmala and signals an inquiry into sāra, the distilled essence beyond vikalpa-bheda, conceptual division. The verse functions as a prelude to the soteriological method of the VBT: moving from doctrinal exposition to direct practice. It also foregrounds the pedagogical pattern of śruti followed by experiential clarification.

speaker: Devi
title: Question About Bhairava’s True Form
sanskrit:
अद्यावप न निवृत्तो मे संशयः परमेश्वर ।
किं रूपं तत्त्वतो देि शब्दराशिकलामयम् ॥ २ ॥
transliteration:
adyāpi na nivṛtto me saṃśayaḥ parameśvara |
kiṃ rūpaṃ tattvato deva śabdarāśikalāmayam || 2 ||
translation: Even now my doubt has not been removed, O Supreme Lord. What is your true form in reality, O Deva, consisting of the multitude of sounds and their portions?
intent_summary: Devi asks Bhairava what his real nature is beyond ordinary description.
beginner_explanation: The Goddess is still unsure and asks a direct question: what is Bhairava really? She hints that he may be made of sound and its subtle parts, but she wants the truth. This invites a teaching that goes beyond words alone.
scholar_explanation: The verse asks for tattvataḥ rūpa, the ontological nature of Bhairava, described as śabdarāśi-kalā-maya—made of the totality of sonic potential and its subdivisions. This frames Bhairava not as a personal deity only, but as the ground of manifest sound and articulation. The inquiry anticipates the VBT's move from cosmological description to contemplative technology.

speaker: Devi
title: Is Bhairava Form or Beyond Form?
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
वकं िा निात्मभेदेन भैरिे भैरिाकृतौ ।
विवशरोभेदवभन्नं िा वकं िा शविियात्मकम् ॥ ३ ॥
transliteration:
kiṃ vā niḥsvaṃ bhedena bhairave bhairavākṛtau |
vivekaro bhedabhinnaṃ vā kiṃ vā śaktiyatmakam || 3 ||
translation: Is it something with difference in Bhairava’s Bhairava-form? Or something divided by differentiation? Or something consisting of Śakti?
intent_summary: Devi probes whether Bhairava is a distinct form, a divided reality, or the nature of power itself.
beginner_explanation: Here the Goddess is testing different possibilities. Is Bhairava a separate shape, a collection of separate parts, or pure energy and power? She is trying to understand whether the divine is one thing or many.
scholar_explanation: The verse contrasts bheda, viveka-bheda, and śaktiyatmaka: whether Bhairava is a delineated form, a differentiated aggregate, or identical with Śakti. This reflects the nondual Śaiva tension between transcendent identity and dynamic power. The inquiry prepares the ground for the teaching that manifestation is neither separate from nor reducible to the absolute.

speaker: Devi
title: Is He Sound, Light, or Wheel?
sanskrit:
नादविन्दुमयं िावप वकं चन्द्राधधवनरोवधका् ।
चक्रारूढमनच्कं िा वकं िा शविस्वरूपकम् ॥ ४ ॥
transliteration:
nādavindumayaṃ vāpi kiṃ candrārdhanirodhikāḥ |
cakrārūḍham anacakraṃ vā kiṃ vā śaktisvarūpakam || 4 ||
translation: Is he perhaps made of sound and bindu? Or of the crescent moon and its arrest? Or mounted on a wheel, yet without a wheel? Or what, in truth, is he as the very nature of Śakti?
intent_summary: Devi asks whether Bhairava should be understood through subtle yogic symbols, sound, or divine power.
beginner_explanation: The Goddess offers more images: a subtle inner sound, a dot of energy, a moon-like point, a wheel, or pure power. She is asking which symbol best points to the divine reality. This shows how hard it is to describe ultimate truth with ordinary language.
scholar_explanation: This verse gathers several tantric markers—nāda, bindu, candra, nirodhikā, cakra—into a single interrogative sequence. These are technical symbols for subtle states, inner processes, and cosmological structures within Śaiva yoga. The verse underscores that Bhairava exceeds any one image while being expressible through them as upāyas.

speaker: Devi
title: Question of Transcendence and Immanence
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
परापरायाः सकलम् अपरायाश्च वा पुनः ।
पराया यदि तद्वत्स्यात् परत्वं तद् विरुध्यते ॥ ५ ॥
transliteration:
parāparāyāḥ sakalam aparāyāś ca vā punaḥ |
parā yadi tadā syāt paratvaṃ tad virudhyate || 5 ||
translation: Is he the totality of the higher and the lower, or only the lower? If he were simply the higher, then his transcendence would be contradicted.
intent_summary: Devi examines whether Bhairava is beyond all levels, within all levels, or only a highest principle.
beginner_explanation: She is asking if the divine includes everything, just the lower levels, or only the highest level. But if he were only the highest, that would limit him too much. So she is pressing toward a more complete understanding.
scholar_explanation: The parāparā/aparā distinction evokes hierarchical levels of reality in Śaiva thought. Devi tests whether Bhairava can be reduced to a single rung of that hierarchy, noting that absolute paratva would be compromised by exclusive identification with one level. The verse thus motivates a nondual synthesis that includes transcendence without exclusion.

speaker: Devi
title: Beyond Letters and Bodies
sanskrit:
न हि वर्णविभेदेन देहभेदेन वा भवेत् ।
परत्वम् निष्कलत्वेन सकलत्वे न तद्भवेत् ॥ ६ ॥
transliteration:
na hi varṇavibhāgena dehabhedena vā bhavet |
paratvam niṣkalatvena sakalatve na tad bhavet || 6 ||
translation: Transcendence cannot arise from division into letters or from division into bodies. It does not exist in the condition of being fragmentary; nor does it belong to the fragmented whole.
intent_summary: Devi rejects any limited definition of the supreme as merely linguistic, bodily, or fragmentary.
beginner_explanation: The Goddess says the highest reality cannot be boxed into pieces, words, or bodies. If something is broken into parts, it is no longer truly absolute. She is ruling out any description that makes the divine too small.
scholar_explanation: This verse denies paratva as a product of varṇa-vibhāga or deha-bheda, rejecting any analysis that objectifies the absolute into parts. The niṣkala/sakala contrast is central to Kashmir Śaivism: the supreme is not a fragmented object, yet manifests as the whole without losing unity. This prepares Bhairava’s corrective teaching by removing conceptual constraints.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Bhairava Welcomes the Inquiry
sanskrit:
प्रसादं कुरु मे नाथ विशेषं विवि संशयम् ।
विज्ञानभैरि तन्त्रम्
साधु साधु त्वया पृष्टं तन्त्रसारवमदं प्रिये ॥ ७ ॥
transliteration:
prasādaṃ kuru me nātha viśeṣaṃ vijiṣaṃśayam |
vijñānabhairi tantram
sādhu sādhu tvayā pṛṣṭaṃ tantrasāram idaṃ priye || 7 ||
translation: Show me grace, Lord, and remove this special doubt. Well done, well done, beloved—you have asked about the very essence of the tantra.
intent_summary: Bhairava praises Devi’s question and prepares to reveal the core teaching.
beginner_explanation: Bhairava responds warmly, saying that her question is exactly the right one. He asks for grace and promises to clear the doubt. This marks the shift from questioning to explanation.
scholar_explanation: Bhairava acknowledges the query as tantrasāra, the essence of the scripture, and thus legitimizes the pedagogical transition. The request for prasāda is conventional yet important: realization is not merely analytical but grace-mediated. The verse also sets a devotional tone while opening the way for the upāya teachings.

speaker: Bhairava
title: The Secret Teaching of Form
sanskrit:
गूहनीयतमं भद्रे तथावप कथयावम ते ।
यविंवचत्सकलम् रूपम् भैरवस्य प्रकीर्तितम् ॥ ८ ॥
transliteration:
gūhanīyatamaṃ bhadre tathāpi kathayāmi te |
yad vijñeyat sakalaṃ rūpaṃ bhairavasya prakīrtitam || 8 ||
translation: Most secret, O fortunate one, yet I will tell it to you: whatever form is to be known as the total form of Bhairava is proclaimed.
intent_summary: Bhairava begins to disclose the hidden truth that all forms point to Bhairava.
beginner_explanation: He says this teaching is very secret, but he will share it anyway. The idea is that all forms can be understood as Bhairava’s form. So the divine is not far away from the world but present in it.
scholar_explanation: The verse introduces the paradox of a guhya teaching made explicit for instruction. Sakala-rūpa here means the total manifested form, which is not separate from Bhairava but one way of speaking of him. This prepares the dhāraṇās by reframing ordinary experience as a contemplative field.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Forms Are Like Illusion
sanskrit:
तदसारतया देवि विज्ञेयं शक्रजालित् ।
मायास्वप्नोपमं चैव गन्धर्वनगरभ्रमम् ॥ ९ ॥
transliteration:
tad asāratayā devi vijñeyaṃ śakrajālavat |
māyāsvapnopamaṃ caiva gandharvanagarabhramam || 9 ||
translation: That should be known, O Goddess, as insubstantial, like an Indra’s net; and likewise like the illusion of māyā, a dream, or the भ्रम of a city of the Gandharvas.
intent_summary: Bhairava teaches that ordinary appearances are vivid yet ultimately insubstantial.
beginner_explanation: He compares the world of forms to a web of reflections, a dream, or a mirage. These things seem real, but they don’t have solid substance. This helps the practitioner loosen their grip on appearances.
scholar_explanation: By invoking śakrajāla, svapna, and gandharvanagara, the text marks phenomenal form as relational and unstable rather than ultimately self-standing. This is not nihilism; it is a recognition of asāratā, allowing consciousness to seek the underlying reality. The imagery also resonates with later Kashmir Śaiva analyses of manifestation as real appearance without independent essence.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Conceptual Thought Is Only a Stopgap
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
ध्यानाथं भ्रान्तिबुद्धीनाम् वक्रयाडम्बरवर्तधनाम् ।
केवलं वर्णितं पुंसां विकल्पवनहतात्मनाम् ॥ १० ॥
transliteration:
dhyānārthaṃ bhrāntibuddhīnāṃ vakrayāḍambaravartadhānām |
kevalaṃ varṇitaṃ puṃsāṃ vikalpavanahatātmanām || 10 ||
translation: For those whose minds are confused and whose ornaments are the display of crooked show, it has been described merely for the sake of meditation—by men whose selves are slain by विकल्प (vikalpa), conceptual thought.
intent_summary: Bhairava says such descriptions are only preliminary aids for minds trapped in conceptuality.
beginner_explanation: He explains that these images and descriptions are tools for people who are confused. They are not the final truth, just stepping-stones for meditation. Once the mind settles, the need for such props fades.
scholar_explanation: This verse limits discursive description to dhyānārtha, instrumental support for minds dominated by vikalpa. The phrase vikalpa-vanaha suggests those entangled or “slain” by conceptual proliferation, for whom symbolic teaching is still necessary. It anticipates the direct methods that bypass conceptual construction in favor of immediate recognition.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Beyond Name, Form, and Composite Identity
sanskrit:
तत्त्वतो न निजात्मासौ शब्दराशिर्न भैरवः ।
न चासौ विविधो देवो न च शक्तिसमात्मकः ॥ ११ ॥
transliteration: tattvato na nijātmāsau śabdarāśir na bhairavaḥ | na cāsau vividho devo na ca śaktisamātmakaḥ || 11 ||
translation: In truth, Bhairava is not the heap of words, nor is he the self as a separate entity. He is not a deity composed of many parts, nor is he constituted as identical with powers in a composite way.
intent_summary: To deny all limited conceptual identities and show that Bhairava cannot be grasped as a constructed object or divided deity.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that the deepest reality is not just a label, idea, or image in the mind. It is not something split into pieces or made up of parts. The teaching points you away from naming and imagining, and toward what is beyond all that.
scholar_explanation: Bhairava is negated as śabdarāśi, a mere aggregate of words, and as nijātman in the sense of a limited individual self. He is also not a vicitra-deva, a multiplicity of deities, nor a composite of śaktis. The verse prepares the listener for a non-objectifiable nondual absolute, consistent with the apophatic method of the VBT.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Beyond Nādabindu and Lunar Restriction
sanskrit:
नादबिन्दुमयो वापि न चन्द्रार्धनिरोधिका् ।
न चक्रक्रमसम्भिन्नो न च शक्तिस्वरूपकः ॥ १२ ॥
transliteration: nādabindumayo vāpi na candrārdhanirodhikāḥ | na cakrakramasambhinno na ca śaktisvarūpakaḥ || 12 ||
translation: He is not made of nada and bindu, nor of the lunar half-circle and its restraint. He is not divided by the क्रम of the chakras, nor is he merely the form of śakti.
intent_summary: To show that even subtle yogic structures and inner phenomena are not the ultimate Bhairava.
beginner_explanation: Here the text says not to mistake special inner experiences for the final truth. Even subtle sounds, energy patterns, or chakra practices are still not the whole reality. They can be helpful, but they are not the destination.
scholar_explanation: The verse rejects identification of Bhairava with nāda-bindu, candrārdha-nirodhikā, cakra-krama, and śakti-svarūpa. These are elements of subtle yogic and tantric praxis, but Bhairava transcends all structured inner phenomena. The teaching protects against reifying meditative signs into the Absolute.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Instruction for the Unready
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
अप्रिुद्धमतीनाम् वह एता िालविभीवषका् ।
मातृमोदकित्सिं प्रिृत्त्यथधमुदाहृतम् ॥ १३ ॥
transliteration: vijñānabhairava tantram | aprabuddhamatīnām vā etāḥ jālavibhīṣikāḥ | mātṛmodakitsintipr̥ttya? unclear due to OCR || 13 ||
translation: This Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra: these are frightening illusions for minds that are not awakened; they are spoken for the sake of those whose activity is still driven by habitual conditioning.
intent_summary: To indicate that the teachings may seem perplexing or alarming to unprepared minds, but are meant as a remedial instruction for practice.
beginner_explanation: This verse warns that these teachings can look strange if your mind is not ready. They are not meant as ordinary philosophy or entertainment. They are given to help people who are still caught in habits and confusion.
scholar_explanation: The OCR is corrupt here, but the sense is an introductory remark on the difficulty of the tantra for aprabuddha or less awakened minds. The dhāraṇās can appear as jāla-vibhīṣikā, a terrifying web or illusion, yet they are introduced as upāya for those still propelled by habitual tendency. This frames the text as a practical, initiatory manual rather than a speculative treatise.

speaker: Bhairava
title: The Unspeakable Supreme Meaning
sanskrit:
वदक्कालकलनोन्मुिा देशोद्देशाविशेवषणी ।
व्यपदेष्टुमशक्यासािकथ्या परमाथधत् ॥ १४ ॥
transliteration: vaktakālakalanonmuktā deśoद्देशaviśeṣiṇī | vyapadeṣṭum aśakyāsā kathyā paramārthataḥ || 14 ||
translation: Freed from the reckoning of time and speech, and distinguishing no particular place or object, she is impossible to describe; yet she is spoken of as the supreme truth.
intent_summary: To affirm that ultimate reality cannot be fully expressed in words, time, or spatial distinctions.
beginner_explanation: This says the highest truth is beyond descriptions like “here,” “there,” “now,” or “later.” Words can point to it, but they cannot capture it. It is like trying to describe the taste of honey to someone who has only read about it.
scholar_explanation: The verse emphasizes that paramārtha is beyond deśa and kāla-kalana, and thus beyond vyapadeśa in ordinary terms. Yet the tantra still speaks of it pedagogically, using language as a provisional pointer. This is characteristic of apophatic nondual Tantric discourse, where speech functions as upāya, not final capture.

speaker: Bhairava
title: The Inner State of Bhairavī
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
अन्त् स्वानुभिानन्दा विकल्पोन्मुिगोचरा ।
यािस्था भवरताकारा भैरिी भैरिात्मन् ॥ १५ ॥
transliteration: antaḥ svānubhavānandā vikalponmuktagocarā | yāvasthā bhairatākārā bhairavī bhairavātman || 15 ||
translation: The state whose inner essence is the bliss of direct self-experience, whose domain is freed from conceptual thought, and whose form is Bhairava-like—that Bhairavī, O Bhairava, is [thus].
intent_summary: To point to a nonconceptual state of self-recognition where bliss and awareness are free of thought-constructs.
beginner_explanation: This verse describes an inner state where you directly feel your own awareness as peaceful and blissful, without constant mental chatter. It is not about thinking harder, but about resting in a clear experience before thoughts take over. The text identifies that state with the goddess Bhairavī.
scholar_explanation: The phrase svānubhavānanda suggests self-luminous experiential bliss, while vikalponmukta-gocara indicates a field beyond vikalpa, conceptual duality. Bhairavī here is not separate from Bhairava but the living mode of his self-awareness. The verse aligns with nondual recognition: the goddess is the experientially manifest aspect of the same absolute consciousness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: The Pure All-Filling Reality
sanskrit:
तद्वपुस्तत्त्वतो ज्ञेयं विमलं विश्वपूरणम् ।
एिं विधे परे तत्त्वे क् पूज्य् कश्च तृप्यवत ॥ १६ ॥
transliteration: tadvapus tattvato jñeyaṃ vimalam viśvapūraṇam | evaṃ vidhe pare tattve kaḥ pūjyaḥ kaś ca tarpyati || 16 ||
translation: That form of his should be known in truth as pure and as pervading all things. In such a supreme reality, who is to be worshiped, and who is to be satisfied?
intent_summary: To direct the practitioner to recognize the absolute as pure, all-pervading consciousness beyond subject-object worship.
beginner_explanation: This verse says the deepest reality is clean, clear, and present in everything. If that is true, then the usual idea of one person worshiping another begins to fall away. There is no separate worshiper and worshiped at the highest level.
scholar_explanation: The tattva is described as vimala and viśvapūraṇa, echoing Kashmir Śaiva descriptions of universal consciousness as stainless and all-encompassing. The rhetorical questions about pūjā and tarpaṇa dissolve dualistic ritual structure in the face of the supreme. This is a nondual shift from external devotion to recognition of pervading awareness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Bhava as the Supreme Goddess
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरि तन्त्रम्
एिं विधा भैरिस्य यािस्था पवरगीयते ।
सा परा पररूपेण परा देिी प्रकीवतधता ॥ १७ ॥
transliteration: evaṃ vidho bhairavasya yāvasthā parigīyate | sā parā parirūpeṇa parā devī prakīrtitā || 17 ||
translation: The state of Bhairava that is spoken of in this way is proclaimed as the supreme Goddess, supreme in the form of all-encompassing totality.
intent_summary: To identify the highest state of Bhairava with the supreme Goddess, showing their nondual identity.
beginner_explanation: The verse says that what is called Bhairava’s highest state is also called the supreme Goddess. In other words, the two are not separate realities. The same truth can be named from either side.
scholar_explanation: The verse explicitly equates Bhairava’s yāvasthā with parā devī in parirūpa, implying a totalizing and inclusive manifestation. This is a classic nondual Śaiva move: consciousness and power, Bhairava and Devī, are two names for one reality. The text thus frames soteriology as recognition of identity rather than union of separate entities.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Always Abiding as Śiva-Śakti Unity
sanskrit:
शविशविमतोयधद्वद् अभेद् सिधदा वस्थत् ।
अतस्तद्धमधवमधत्वात् पराशवि् परात्मन् ॥ १८ ॥
transliteration: śaktiśaktimatoḥ yadvad abhedaḥ sarvadā sthitaḥ | asti tad dharmadharmatvāt parāśaktiḥ parātman || 18 ||
translation: Just as power and the possessor of power are always established as non-different, so, by the nature of dharma and its bearer, the supreme power is the supreme Self.
intent_summary: To teach that śakti and śaktimān are inseparable, grounding nonduality in their constant identity.
beginner_explanation: This verse uses a simple example: power and the one who has power are not really separate. In the same way, consciousness and its energy are one reality. The point is to help you stop splitting experience into two disconnected things.
scholar_explanation: The verse states the perennial abheda of śakti and śaktimān, then extends the analogy to parāśakti as parātman. The wording dharma-dharmitva suggests inseparability as a property and its bearer, an ontological mutual implication. This is central to Kashmir Shaivism, where awareness (prakāśa) and power (vimarśa) are two aspects of one absolute.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Entry Through Pure Awareness
sanskrit:
न िह्नेदाधवहका शविव्यधवतवरिा विभाव्यते ।
केिलम् ज्ञानसत्तायां प्रारम्भोऽयं प्रिेशने ॥ १९ ॥
transliteration: na vahner ādāhika śaktir vyatiriktā vibhāvyate | kevalam jñānasattāyāṃ prārambho 'yaṃ praveśane || 19 ||
translation: The burning power of fire is not contemplated as separate from fire. Likewise, this beginning is only an entry into the being of knowledge alone.
intent_summary: To establish that the practice begins from the inseparability of awareness and its power, leading into direct realization.
beginner_explanation: Fire and its heat are not two separate things, and the verse says awareness works the same way. Practice begins by entering directly into clear knowing itself, rather than hunting for something outside it. You start from the light of awareness that is already present.
scholar_explanation: The analogy of fire and its dāhika-śakti illustrates that śakti is intrinsic, not extrinsic, to its source. The verse then shifts to jñāna-sattā as the point of entry, indicating that the dhāraṇās operate from awareness itself rather than from objectified techniques. This prepares for methods in which recognition of consciousness is the means and end.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Entering the Śaiva State Through Energy
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
शक्त्यिस्थाप्रविष्टस्य वनविधभागेन भािना ।
तदासौ वशिरूपी स्यात् शैिी मुखवमहोच्यते ॥ २० ॥
transliteration: śaktyavasthāpraviṣṭasya nirvibhāgena bhāvanā | tadāsau śivarūpī syāt śaivī mukham ihocyate || 20 ||
translation: For one who has entered the state of śakti, contemplation without division arises. Then that one becomes Śiva-shaped; here this is called the Śaiva approach.
intent_summary: To instruct the practitioner to enter the energetic state without division so that meditation ripens into identity with Śiva.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that when you settle into the living energy of experience without dividing it up, the result is a sense of being wholly one with the divine. You do not force this; you let experience become simple and undivided. That undivided way of entering is called the Śaiva method.
scholar_explanation: Śakty-avasthā-praveśa here denotes immersion into the dynamic aspect of consciousness, followed by nirvibhāga-bhāvanā, nonsegmenting contemplation. The outcome, śivarūpī, indicates transformation through recognition rather than a produced state. The phrase śaivī mukham identifies this as a principal Tantric entrance to nondual realization.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Light Reveals the Lamp and Sun
sanskrit:
यथालोकेन दीपस्य वकरणैभाधस्करस्य च ।
ज्ञायते वदवविभागावद तद्वच्छक्त्या वशि् वप्रये ॥ २१ ॥
transliteration:
yathālokena dīpasya kārakair bhāskarasya ca |
jñāyate bhedavibhāgāvad tadvat śaktyā vśi priye || 21 ||
translation: Just as by the light of a lamp or by the rays of the sun its distinct parts are known, so too, O beloved, is this known by Śakti through her power.
intent_summary: Use the illuminating power of awareness to perceive distinctions without losing the underlying unity.
beginner_explanation: A lamp and the sun make things visible. In the same way, this verse says that consciousness can reveal the differences in experience while still being the light that makes all experience known. The point is to notice awareness itself, not just the things it illuminates.
scholar_explanation: The verse uses the analogy of dīpa-prabhā and sūrya-kiraṇa to indicate that differentiated cognition arises within a single luminous principle. Śakti is the manifesting power by which bheda-vibhāga becomes knowable, yet the knowing light remains one. This supports the non-dual epistemology of the VBT: distinctions are apparent within consciousness, not outside it.

speaker: Devi
title: Devi Describes the Formless Bhairava
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरि तन्त्रम्
देिदेि विशूलाङ्क कपालकृतभूषण ।
वदवदेशकालशून्या च व्यपदेशवििवजधता ॥ २२ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantraṃ |
devi devi viśūlāṅka kapālakṛtabhūṣaṇa |
bhedadeśakālaśūnyā ca vyapadeśavivarjitā || 22 ||
translation: O Goddess, O Goddess, marked with the trident, adorned with a skull-garland: you are empty of division, place, and time, and beyond all designation.
intent_summary: Present Bhairava/Devi as beyond time, space, and conceptual labeling in order to point toward the non-dual absolute.
beginner_explanation: This verse praises the Goddess as beyond ordinary boundaries like place and time. It says the deepest reality cannot be pinned down with labels. The aim is to turn the mind away from fixed ideas and toward what cannot be named.
scholar_explanation: Devi is addressed through iconographic epithets—viśūlāṅka and kapālakṛta-bhūṣaṇa—while simultaneously being defined apophatically as bheda-deśa-kāla-śūnya and vyapadeśa-vivarjitā. This is classic Tantric paradox: the deity is both vividly manifest and beyond all limiting predicates. The verse prepares the doctrinal ground for the dhāraṇās by negating spatial-temporal objectification.

speaker: Devi
title: Devi Asks How Bhairava Is Realized
sanskrit:
यािस्था भवरताकारा भैरवस्योपलभ्यते ।
कैरुपायैर्मुखम् तस्य परा देवि कथं भवेत् ।
यथा सम्यगहम् देवि तथा मे ब्रूवह भैरव ॥ २३ ॥
transliteration:
yāvasthā bhairavākārā bhairavasyopalabhyate |
kair upāyair mukhaṃ tasya parā devi kathaṃ bhavet |
yathā samyag ahaṃ devi tathā me brūhi bhairava || 23 ||
translation: Whatever state is perceived as having the form of Bhairava—by what means does one approach his face, O supreme Goddess? Tell me correctly, O Goddess, how it is, O Bhairava.
intent_summary: Ask for the practical means by which the form of Bhairava is directly realized.
beginner_explanation: Here the speaker asks a very practical question: if Bhairava is something one can somehow experience, how does one get there? It is like asking for the method, not just the philosophy. This question leads directly into the meditation instructions.
scholar_explanation: This verse shifts from doctrinal description to soteriological inquiry: yā avasthā bhairavākārā is the perceptible state that indexes Bhairava, and the question is for upāya, the means of approach. The phrase mukhaṃ tasya suggests direct access or face-to-face realization, not indirect belief. It functions as the gateway into the 112 dhāraṇās.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Raising and Filling with Breath
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
ऊर्ध्वे प्राणो ह्यधो जीवो विसर्गात्मा परोच्चरेत् ।
उत्पत्तिविधयस्थाने भरणाद्भवता स्थिति् ॥ २४ ॥
transliteration:
ūrdhve prāṇo hy adho jīvo visargātmā paroccaret |
utpattividhisthāne bharaṇād bhavataḥ sthitiḥ || 24 ||
translation: When prāṇa rises upward, the jīva goes downward; the supreme emerges as visarga. In the place of arising, through filling or sustaining, there is your abiding presence.
intent_summary: Direct awareness to the movement of prāṇa and the pause or fullness that reveals stable presence.
beginner_explanation: This verse points to the breath as a doorway. When you notice energy rising and falling, there is a moment where the usual sense of ‘me’ softens. By resting in that pause or fullness, you can sense a deeper stillness beneath breathing.
scholar_explanation: The verse contrasts ūrdhva-prāṇa and adho-jīva, indicating a reversal or transcendence of ordinary embodied identification. Visarga here can be read as the outflow or emanative release of consciousness, while bharaṇa suggests sustaining the interval where manifestation arises. The dhāraṇā is to dwell in the utpatti-sthāna, the generative junction, where sthiti as Bhairava is disclosed.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Inner Offering in the Void
sanskrit:
मरुतोऽन्तर्हविः वा वियद्युमावनितधनात् ।
भैरव्या भैरवस्येत्थं भैरवि व्यज्यते वपुः ॥ २५ ॥
transliteration:
maruto 'ntar havir vā viyad yuvā manitadhanāt |
bhairavyā bhairavasyetthaṃ bhairavi vyajyate vapuḥ || 25 ||
translation: The winds, the inner oblation, or the sky—by these, O Bhairavī, the body of Bhairava is manifested in this way.
intent_summary: Contemplate the inner elements of breath, offering, and space as ways the divine body reveals itself.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that you can experience the sacred body through inner breath, inner offering, or spacious awareness. Instead of looking for something outside, you notice what is happening inside your own experience. The body of Bhairava is disclosed in those subtle inner realities.
scholar_explanation: Marutaḥ, havis, and viyat point respectively to breath currents, inner oblation, and etheric spaciousness as loci of tantric vision. The divine body (vapus) is not a gross object but a subtle manifestation recognized through internalized ritual perception. This verse bridges outer yajña imagery with the contemplative interiorization characteristic of Kaula and Trika practice.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Neither Going Nor Entering
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
न व्रजेन्न विशेच्छविमधरुद्रूपा विकावसते ।
वनविधकल्पतया मध्ये तया भैरिरूपता ॥ २६ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantraṃ |
na vrajennā viśec chāvim adharūpaṃ vikāvasate |
vanavidhiprāptatayā madhye tayā bhairarūpatā || 26 ||
translation: One should neither go forth nor enter into a form lower than the radiance; by the method of the forest-path, in the middle, the nature of Bhairava is revealed.
intent_summary: Rest in the middle without moving toward or away from appearances, and Bhairava-nature is revealed.
beginner_explanation: This verse tells you not to chase after experiences and not to push them away. Instead, stay in the middle, like walking a path through a forest without getting lost to either side. In that balanced stillness, the divine nature shows itself.
scholar_explanation: The instruction negates both outward projection (vrajet) and inward fixation (viśet), indicating a nondual middle that is not a compromise but the very locus of revelation. The obscure phrase about vanavidhi implies an indirect yet natural path where one remains in the center rather than extremizing cognition. Bhairarūpatā emerges in madhya, a key Trika motif echoed throughout the text.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Resting at the End of Breath
sanskrit:
कुवम्भता रेवचता िावप पूर्वता िा यदा भिेत् ।
तदन्ते शान्तनामासौ शक्त्या शान्त् प्रकाशते ॥ २७ ॥
transliteration:
kumbhatā recakatā vāpi pūrvakā vā yadā bhavet |
tadante śāntanāmā sau śaktyā śāntiḥ prakāśate || 27 ||
translation: When there is kumbhaka, recaka, or pūraka, then at their end the one called Peace shines forth through Śakti.
intent_summary: Use the endings of inhalation, exhalation, or retention to enter the luminous peace beyond breath.
beginner_explanation: Breathing has natural stopping points: after inhaling, after exhaling, and during the pause itself. This verse says those small gaps are important because peace can become obvious there. It invites you to notice the stillness at the end of each breath.
scholar_explanation: Kumbhaka, recaka, and pūraka denote the principal breath phases; the instruction focuses not on the phases themselves but on their ante, the endpoint where śānti manifests. Śakti is the revealing power by which the state named Śānta becomes luminous. This is one of the classic VBT breath-junction methods that leverages temporal discontinuity to open onto awareness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Contemplating the Rising Subtle Radiance
sanskrit:
आमूलाविरणाभासां सूक्ष्मात् सूक्ष्मतरावत्मकाम् ।
वचन्तयेत्ताम् वद्वषट्कान्ते श्याम्यन्तीम् भैरवोदयः ॥ २८ ॥
transliteration:
āmūlāvirbhāsaṃ sūkṣmāt sūkṣmatarātmakam |
cintayet tāṃ dvyaṣaṭkānte śāmyantīṃ bhairavodayaḥ || 28 ||
translation: One should contemplate that radiance shining from the root, whose essence is subtler than the subtle, as it subsides at the end of the thirty-two; there is the arising of Bhairava.
intent_summary: Visualize a very subtle inner radiance and follow it as it subsides into stillness until Bhairava dawns.
beginner_explanation: Imagine a delicate light growing from deep inside, so subtle that it is almost beyond description. The verse says to keep your attention on that light as it quiets down. In that soft fading, a deeper presence appears.
scholar_explanation: The dhāraṇā directs contemplation toward āmūla-āvirbhāsa, an emergent luminosity from the root that is sūkṣmāt sūkṣmatara, i.e., progressively subtler than subtle objectivity. The mention of dvyaṣaṭka may encode a numeric threshold or internal locus of contemplative completion; as the radiance śāmyati, Bhairavodaya occurs. The method is visual-luminous but culminates in non-objective awareness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Ascending Lightning Path
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरि तन्त्रम्
उद्गच्छन्तं तवडद्रूपाम् प्रवतचक्रं क्रमात्क्रमम् ।
ऊर्ध्वं मुवष्टियं याित् तािदन्ते महोदय् ॥ २९ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantraṃ |
udgacchantīṃ tvaḍdṛpām prāvṛtacakraṃ kramāt kramam |
ūrdhvaṃ muṣṭiṃ yāvat tāvad ante mahodayaḥ || 29 ||
translation: Seeing it rise like lightning through the wheel in sequence and step by step, until it reaches upward to the fist, at the end there is great emergence.
intent_summary: Follow a lightning-like upward movement through the inner channels until a great awakening occurs.
beginner_explanation: This verse uses the image of lightning moving upward very quickly. You pay attention to an inner rising energy or light as it moves through stages. When it reaches its culmination, a big opening or awakening happens.
scholar_explanation: The imagery of tvaṭ/vidyut-like rising suggests a swift, vertical contemplative ascent through the cakra sequence. The verse pairs sequential movement (krama) with a culminating mahodaya, indicating that structured visualization can lead to a sudden expansion beyond structure. The reference to muṣṭi may encode an embodied endpoint or seal in the upper body.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Twelvefold Completion of the Pattern
sanskrit:
क्रमद्वादशकं सम्यग् द्वादशाक्षरभेवदतम् ।
स्थूलसूक्ष्मपरवस्थत्या मुक्त्वा मुक्त्वान्तत् वशि् ॥ ३० ॥
transliteration:
kramadvādaśakaṃ samyag dvādaśākṣarabhāvitam |
sthūlasūkṣmaparasthityā muktvā muktvāntataḥ śivaḥ || 30 ||
translation: The twelvefold sequence, duly cultivated through the twelve syllables, is released again and again through gross, subtle, and supreme states, until finally Śiva remains.
intent_summary: Use a twelve-step contemplative sequence to progressively release identification with all levels until only Śiva remains.
beginner_explanation: This verse speaks of a repeated sequence that you work through carefully. As you move from the obvious and physical to the subtle and beyond, you keep letting go. In the end, what remains is pure divine presence.
scholar_explanation: Kramadvādaśaka and dvādaśākṣara likely refer to a twelvefold contemplative pattern linked to mantra and internal stages, though the OCR is difficult. The central instruction is repeated relinquishment—muktvā muktvā—across sthūla, sūkṣma, and para states, culminating in identification with Śiva. This is explicit laya logic: dissolution through progressive deconstruction of layered cognition.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Rising Through the Brow-Apex Bridge
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
तयापूयाधशु मूर्धान्तं भङ्क्त्वा भ्रूक्षेपसेतुना ।
वनविधकल्पं मन् कृत्वा सिरूर्ध्वे सिधगोद्गम् ॥ ३१ ॥
transliteration: tayāpūyādhaśu mūrdhāntaṃ bhaṅktvā bhṛkṣepasetunā | vanavidhakalpaṃ man kṛtvā sirūrdhve sidhagodgam || 31 ||
translation: Having pierced the crown-apex by the bridge of the brow-raising (bhru-kṣepa), and making the mind like a forest-ridden course, one should ascend upward to the head.|| 31 ||
intent_summary: Use the upward force of attention at the brow to break through into the crown and direct the mind upward.
beginner_explanation: This verse asks you to lift attention from the forehead toward the top of the head. The idea is like opening a gate above the usual field of thinking and letting awareness rise. It uses a subtle body focus rather than ordinary reasoning.
scholar_explanation: The practice employs bhru-kṣepa, the upward movement or “bridge” of the brows, to pierce the mūrdhānta, the crown-apex. The imagery of the mind becoming vanavidhakalpa suggests a winding, forest-like inward route that is then transcended by ascent to the upper center. It belongs to the VBT’s nāḍī/subtle-center contemplations, where attention is stabilized upward toward a higher state of consciousness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Fivefold Void Contemplation
sanskrit:
वशवखपक्षैवश्चिरूपैमण्डलै् शून्यपञ्चकम् ।
ध्यायतोऽनुत्तरे शून्ये प्रिेशो हृदये भिेत् ॥ ३२ ॥
transliteration: vaśa vakha pakṣai vaścirūpaimaṇḍalaiḥ śūnyapañcakam | dhyāyato'nuttare śūnye prīeśo hṛdaye bhavet || 32 ||
translation: By meditating on the five voids through the controlled forms, wings, and circles, entry into the unsurpassed void arises in the heart.|| 32 ||
intent_summary: Contemplate layered emptiness until the heart opens into the highest void.
beginner_explanation: This verse points to meditating on several levels of emptiness, not just blankness. Imagine looking through successive open spaces until you feel an inner vastness in the heart. The practice aims to make emptiness feel alive and present.
scholar_explanation: The verse speaks of śūnyapañcaka, the “five voids,” approached through nānā-rūpa-maṇḍala imagery and dhyāna. By sustained contemplation of these graded spaces, one enters the anuttara-śūnya, the unsurpassed void, which is not mere absence but the luminous openness of the heart (hṛdaya). This reflects the Trika valuation of śūnyatā as a doorway to the nondual center rather than nihilistic emptiness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Absorption in the Supreme Void
sanskrit:
ईदृशेन क्रमेणैि यि कुिावप वचन्तना ।
शून्ये कुड्ये परे पािे स्वयम् लीना िरप्रदा ॥ ३३ ॥
transliteration: īdṛśena krameṇai vi ya ki kunāvapa vchanatanā | śūnye kuḍye pare pāe svayam līnā varapradā || 33 ||
translation: By such a क्रम (sequence), whatever thought arises anywhere becomes itself dissolved in the void-wall, the supreme side; thus the boon-giving one is absorbed by itself.|| 33 ||
intent_summary: Let all arising thought dissolve on its own into the surrounding void until only absorption remains.
beginner_explanation: Here the instruction is to notice any thought and let it melt into open space instead of following it. It is like writing on water: the thought appears, then disappears without a trace. The result is a natural sinking into stillness.
scholar_explanation: This dhāraṇā extends śūnya-bhāvanā by allowing any vikalpa or ordinary mentation to be dissolved in the pare pāre, the “other” or transcendent side, figured as a void-wall. The language of svayam līnā emphasizes spontaneous laya rather than forced suppression. The verse highlights a core Tantric move: all mental content is used as fuel for its own self-dissolution in the transcendent.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Fixing the Gaze at the Cranium
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
कपालान्तमधनो न्यस्य वतष्ठन्मीवलतलोचन् ।
क्रमेण मनसो दार्ढ्यात् लक्षयेत् लक्ष्यं उत्तमम् ॥ ३४ ॥
transliteration: vijñānabhairava tantram | kapālāntam adhano nyasya tiṣṭhan mīlitalochan | krameṇa manaso dārḍhyāt lakṣayet lakṣyam uttamam || 34 ||
translation: Placing the lower end at the tip of the skull and standing with closed eyes, one should, by gradually strengthening the mind, aim at the supreme object.|| 34 ||
intent_summary: Stabilize the mind through a precise inner target centered at the skull and sustain attention until it becomes strong.
beginner_explanation: This practice asks you to sit quietly with eyes closed and hold attention on a specific inner point near the top of the head. You gradually make the mind steadier, like training a flashlight to stay fixed on one spot. Over time, the focus itself becomes meditative.
scholar_explanation: The verse prescribes kapālānta placement and mīlitalochana, closed-eye concentration, to cultivate manaso dārḍhya, mental firmness. Lakṣya here is the supreme target, likely the upper subtle focus associated with the crown or a central bindu. The method belongs to dhāraṇā via one-pointed fixation, preparing the mind for entry into higher awareness without discursive fluctuation.

speaker: Bhairava
title: The Central Channel of Light
sanskrit:
मध्यनाडी मध्यसंस्था विससूत्राभरूपया ।
ध्यातान्तव्योमया देव्या तया देवि प्रकाशते ॥ ३५ ॥
transliteration: madhyanāḍī madhyasaṃsthā viśvasūtrābhirūpaya | dhyātāntarvyomayā devyā tayā deve prakāśate || 35 ||
translation: The middle channel, situated in the center, has the form of the thread of the universe; by that inner-space-form Goddess, the God shines forth.|| 35 ||
intent_summary: Meditate on the central channel as the luminous axis through which divine awareness becomes manifest.
beginner_explanation: This verse tells you to sense a central line running through the body, like a thread connecting everything. When attention rests there, the divine brightness becomes apparent. It is like finding the vertical axis of a wheel and recognizing the whole wheel through it.
scholar_explanation: The madhyanāḍī is presented as viśvasūtra, the thread of the universe, a classic Trika image linking the inner channel to cosmic structure. The dhyātāntarvyomayā devī indicates the Goddess as inner space, whose contemplation reveals prakāśa in Deva. This verse integrates subtle anatomy with the doctrine that consciousness manifests through a central, nondual axis.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Gaze into the Bindu
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
कररुद्धदृगस्त्रेण भ्रूभेदाद्द्वाररोधनात् ।
दृष्टे विन्दौ क्रमाल्लीने तन्मध्ये परमा वस्थवत् ॥ ३६ ॥
transliteration: vijñānabhairava tantram | kararuddhadṛgastreṇa bhūrbhedād dvārarodhanāt | dṛṣṭe bindau kramāl līne tanmadhye paramāvasthitiḥ || 36 ||
translation: By the gaze restrained with the hand, by closing the doorway through the breaking of the brow-division, when the bindu is seen and gradually dissolved, supreme abiding occurs in that middle.|| 36 ||
intent_summary: Use a fixed, blocked gaze to perceive the bindu and let it dissolve into the supreme middle state.
beginner_explanation: This verse describes preventing the eyes from scattering outward so attention can settle on a tiny point of light or focus. As that point becomes steady and then fades, a deeper stillness appears. Think of watching a candle until the flame is no longer separate from the darkness around it.
scholar_explanation: The practice combines kara-ruddha-dṛg, a restrained gaze, with bhūr-bheda and dvāra-rodhana, sealing the sensory gate at the brow. The dṛṣṭe bindau is the visual apprehension of the subtle point, which then dissolves (līna) to reveal paramāvasthiti, the supreme station or abidance. This is a standard bindu-dhyāna technique in the VBT, turning visual fixation into nondual absorption.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Dissolving the Point into the Heart
sanskrit:
धामान्त् क्षोभसम्भूतसूक्ष्माविवतलकाकृवतम् ।
विन्दुं वशखान्ते हृदये लयान्ते ध्यायतो लय् ॥ ३७ ॥
transliteration: dhāmānt kṣobhasambhūtasūkṣmāvitatalākṛtim | binduṃ vaśakhānte hṛdaye layānte dhyāyato layaḥ || 37 ||
translation: Meditating on the bindu, subtle and expanded in form, born of a stirring in the sphere of light, at the end of the palate and in the heart at the end of dissolution, there is absorption.|| 37 ||
intent_summary: Contemplate the subtle bindu as it expands and sinks into the heart until meditation culminates in laya.
beginner_explanation: This verse uses a tiny inner point as an anchor, then lets that point expand and settle into the heart. The point is not forced; it naturally melts into stillness. It is similar to tracing a drop of water until it merges back into the ocean.
scholar_explanation: The bindu is described as arising from dhāma, the luminous sphere, and appearing as a subtle extended form. Attention is placed at the vaśakhānta, the end of the palate, and in the hṛdaya, where laya occurs. The verse shows the VBT’s recurring pattern of moving from a concrete subtle object to absorption in the heart, the seat of awakened awareness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Attuning to the Unstruck Sound
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
अनाहते पािकणेऽभिशब्दे सवरद्द्रुते ।
शब्दब्रह्मवण वनष्णात् परं ब्रह्मावधगच्छवत ॥ ३८ ॥
transliteration: vijñānabhairava tantram | anāhate pāvakhaṇe'bhīśabde svaraddhṛte | śabdabrahmaviniṣṇātāt paraṃ brahmādhigacchati || 38 ||
translation: In the unstruck, piercing inner sound and in the held resonance of the tone, one who is well-versed in sound-Brahman attains the supreme Brahman.|| 38 ||
intent_summary: Listen inwardly to the subtle unstruck sound until it leads beyond sound to the supreme absolute.
beginner_explanation: Instead of listening to outside noise, this practice asks you to notice the faint inner hum or ringing that can appear in silence. You stay with it until awareness becomes very still and deep. The sound is used as a doorway, not as the final goal.
scholar_explanation: The verse refers to anāhata, the unstruck sound, and abhiśabda/svaraddhṛta, subtle resonant tone or held sound, as an object of contemplation. Mastery of śabdabrahman leads to paraṃ brahma, indicating that inner sonority is a transitional support, not the terminus. This is a classic nāda-upāsanā in Tantra, where sonic vibration is refined into transcendent realization.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Breath into the Void
sanskrit:
प्रणिावदसमुच्चारात् प्लुतान्ते शून्यभािानात् ।
शून्यया परया शक्त्या शून्यतामेवत भैरवि ॥ ३९ ॥
transliteration: praṇavādisamuccārāt plutānte śūnyabhāvanāt | śūnyayā parayā śaktyā śūnyatām eti bhairavi || 39 ||
translation: From the utterance of Oṃ and similar sounds, at the end of the prolonged exhalation, by contemplating emptiness, O Bhairavī, one attains emptiness through the supreme śakti of emptiness.|| 39 ||
intent_summary: Use the pause at the end of a prolonged breath and sound to enter emptiness through contemplation.
beginner_explanation: This verse connects chanting or sounding with the pause after a long breath or syllable. In that pause, you rest in emptiness instead of rushing to the next breath. It is like noticing the quiet gap after a bell rings.
scholar_explanation: The practice links praṇava (and analogous utterance) with plutānta, the end of an elongated utterance/breath, and śūnya-bhāvanā. The “supreme śakti of emptiness” (parā śūnyā śakti) suggests that emptiness is dynamic and power-filled, not inert. This verse unites sonic recitation and breath suspension with śūnya realization, a key VBT junction practice.

speaker: Bhairava
title: The Empty Form of Thought
sanskrit:
यस्य कस्यावप िणधस्य पूिाधन्तािनुभाियेत् ।
शून्यया शून्यभूतोऽसौ शून्याकार् पुमान्भिेत् ॥ ४० ॥
transliteration: yasya kasyāpi varṇasya pūrvāntāvanubhāvayet | śūnyayā śūnyabhūto'sau śūnyākāraḥ pumān bhavet || 40 ||
translation: Whatever sound or letter one contemplates from beginning to end, that person becomes empty through emptiness and takes on the form of emptiness.|| 40 ||
intent_summary: Contemplate any sound or letter thoroughly until the meditator becomes empty like the object itself.
beginner_explanation: Choose a sound, syllable, or letter and follow it from start to finish with complete attention. Then let your sense of being a separate watcher fade into the same stillness as the sound. It is like becoming quiet enough to match the silence you are hearing.
scholar_explanation: The verse generalizes mantra or varṇa contemplation: any phoneme can serve as a vessel if followed through its beginning and end. By śūnyā, the practitioner becomes śūnyabhūta and assumes śūnyākāra, the form of emptiness, indicating identity with the void rather than mere observation. This is a radical Tantric claim that even linguistic units can dissolve subject-object structure when fully penetrated.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Inner Sound Beyond the Last Syllable
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
तन्त्र्यावदिाद्यशब्देषु दीघेषु क्रमसवम्स्थते् ।
अनन्यचेता् प्रत्यन्ते परव्योमिपुभधिेत् ॥ ४१ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantraṃ
vanyadvādyādiśabdeṣu dīrgheṣu kramasamutthite |
ananyacetāḥ pratyante paravyomni budhyet || 41 ||
translation: In the long, progressively arising sounds of instruments and other sounds, with one-pointed mind, one should realize the supreme space at the end.
intent_summary: Attend to long external sound until it naturally dissolves into the silent supreme expanse beyond it.
beginner_explanation: Listen to a long sound, like a sustained note or hum, and keep your attention on it until it fades. At the moment it ends, notice the stillness that remains. The practice is to recognize that silence is not empty in a dead way, but full and alive.
scholar_explanation: This dhāraṇā uses āhata-nāda, external sound, as a doorway to paravyoman, the transcendent space beyond differentiated perception. By maintaining ananyacetas, the practitioner follows the sound’s gradual emergence and dissolution until the residual awareness of silence is revealed. This aligns with VBT methods that use sensory phenomena as supports for immediate recognition of nondual consciousness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Mantra Dissolving into Void
sanskrit:
वपण्डमन्त्रस्य सिधस्य स्थूलिणधक्रमेण तु ।
अधेन्दुविन्दुनादान्त् शून्योच्चाराद्भिेवच्छि् ॥ ४२ ॥
transliteration:
piṇḍamantrasya siddhasya sthūlakṣarakramaṇena tu |
ardhendu-bindunādānte śūnyoccārād bhavecchivaḥ || 42 ||
translation: For a perfected mantra of a single syllable (piṇḍa-mantra), by the क्रम of its gross letters, and through the ending of crescent, bindu, and nāda, one becomes Śiva by uttering it as void.
intent_summary: Use mantra to pass beyond its letters, sound-points, and resonance into the silent source from which it arises.
beginner_explanation: Here the verse says to move through a mantra carefully, but not stop at the words. Let the sound unfold until even its subtle parts disappear into silence. When the mantra is released as emptiness, identity shifts from doing the practice to resting as the awareness behind it.
scholar_explanation: The verse describes the internalization of piṇḍa-mantra by tracing its gross akṣara-sequence toward the subtle phases of ardhendu, bindu, and nāda, then ending in śūnya-uccāra, utterance as void. This reflects the tantric logic that mantra is not merely semantic but a vibration whose subtler strata disclose the nondual ground. The culmination as śivaḥ indicates recognition rather than production of divinity.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Simultaneous Visualization of the Body as Universe
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरि तन्त्रम्
वनजदेहे सिधवदक्कम् युगपद्भाियेवद्वयत् ।
वनविधकल्पमनास्तस्य वियत्सिधम् प्रितधते ॥ ४३ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantraṃ
nijadehe siddhavatkaṃ yaugapad bhāvayed dvayat |
nirvikalpa-manās tasya viyat-siddhiṃ pravartate || 43 ||
translation: In one’s own body, one should simultaneously envision it as already perfected, as the duality-free one. For such a person whose mind is without conceptualization, the accomplishment of space arises.
intent_summary: See the body as already complete and identical with the nondual expanse so the mind becomes free of division.
beginner_explanation: Instead of thinking of your body as ordinary and limited, imagine it as already whole and awakened. Hold this vision without comparing or analyzing it. When that habit of mental labeling drops away, a sense of vastness and freedom can appear.
scholar_explanation: The verse combines body-centered contemplation with yaugapad-bhāvanā, simultaneous recognition, and nirvikalpa-manas, mind free from conceptual construction. The body (nijadeha) is not rejected but re-seen as siddhavac, as if already perfected, revealing viyat-siddhi, attainment of space or vastness. The practice parallels VBT’s recurring insistence that the phenomenal locus itself is the site of liberation.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Double Void of Back and Root
sanskrit:
पृष्टशून्यम् मूलशून्यम् युगपद्भाियेच्च य् ।
शरीरवनरपेवक्षण्या शक्त्या शून्यमना भिेत् ॥ ४४ ॥
transliteration:
pṛṣṭaśūnyaṃ mūlaśūnyaṃ yugapad bhāvayecca yaḥ |
śarīranirapekṣiṇyā śaktyā śūnyamanā bhavet || 44 ||
translation: One who simultaneously contemplates the void behind and the void at the root becomes mind-as-void through the power that is independent of the body.
intent_summary: Contemplate emptiness simultaneously in two bodily directions until mind itself takes on the quality of void.
beginner_explanation: Feel the space behind you and the space at the base of the body at the same time. Do not tense up or try to force anything. As attention opens in both directions, the mind can become quiet and spacious.
scholar_explanation: Pṛṣṭaśūnya and mūlaśūnya designate two polar loci of śūnyatā within embodied awareness, likely rear and base. The verse emphasizes śarīra-nirapekṣiṇī śakti, a power not dependent on the gross body, indicating an energetic opening beyond somatic fixation. The result is śūnyamanas, a mind resonant with emptiness rather than conceptuality.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Threefold Void Contemplation
sanskrit:
पृष्टशून्यं मूलशून्यं हृच्छून्यं भाियेविरम् ।
युगपवन्नविधकल्पत्वावन्नविधकल्पोदयस्तत् ॥ ४५ ॥
transliteration:
pṛṣṭaśūnyaṃ mūlaśūnyaṃ hṛcchūnyaṃ bhāvayet sadā |
yugapannirvikalpatvān nirvikalpodayas tataḥ || 45 ||
translation: One should always contemplate the void of the back, the void of the root, and the void of the heart. By simultaneous freedom from conceptualization, the arising of the non-conceptual then occurs.
intent_summary: Open awareness to multiple inner voids at once so conceptual thought gives way to direct, nonconceptual knowing.
beginner_explanation: Think of the space behind the body, the base of the body, and the heart area all at once. Don’t turn these into ideas; simply feel openness. When you stop mentally naming things, a fresh, quiet awareness can surface on its own.
scholar_explanation: This dhāraṇā extends the previous verse by adding hṛcchūnya, the void of the heart, forming a triadic spatial contemplative field. The yaugapadya of these contemplations destabilizes vikalpa, allowing nirvikalpa to arise spontaneously. It exemplifies the VBT strategy of transforming ordinary spatial perception into the recognition of consciousness as open, undivided field.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Momentary Emptiness in the Body
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
तनूदेशे शून्यतैि क्षणमािं विभाियेत् ।
वनविधकल्पं वनविधकल्पो वनविधकल्पस्वरूपभाक् ॥ ४६ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantraṃ
tanūdeśe śūnyataiva kṣaṇamātraṃ vibhāvayet |
nirvikalpo nirvikalpo nirvikalpasvarūpabhāk || 46 ||
translation: In the region of the body, one should contemplate emptiness for only a moment. Being without conceptualization, one becomes one who partakes of the nature of the nonconceptual.
intent_summary: Briefly touch the body with the sense of emptiness until the mind slips into its own nonconceptual nature.
beginner_explanation: Notice a tiny pause of openness somewhere in the body, even if it lasts only a second. Don’t try to extend it by force. Just recognize that even a brief glimpse of emptiness can reveal a deeper, quiet awareness.
scholar_explanation: The emphasis on kṣaṇamātra shows that even a fleeting encounter with śūnyatā in tanūdeśa can be decisive. The repeated nirvikalpa underscores the verse’s claim that the practitioner does not manufacture insight but recognizes nirvikalpasvarūpabhāk, participation in the nature of nonconceptual consciousness. This is a classic VBT move: the smallest interval becomes a portal to the absolute.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Body Filled with Space
sanskrit:
सिं देहगतं द्रव्यं वियद्व्याप्तं मृगेक्षणे ।
विभाियेत्ततस्तस्य भािना सा वस्थरा भिेत् ॥ ४७ ॥
transliteration:
sarvaṃ dehagataṃ dravyaṃ viyadvyāptaṃ mṛgekṣaṇe |
vibhāvayettataḥ tasya bhāvanā sā sthirā bhavet || 47 ||
translation: O doe-eyed one, one should visualize all substances present in the body as pervaded by space; then that contemplation becomes steady.
intent_summary: See every part of the body as filled with space until that perception becomes stable and continuous.
beginner_explanation: Imagine your body not as a solid block, but as full of open space. Let this include bones, organs, and skin without fighting the image. If you keep returning to this view, it can become steady and natural.
scholar_explanation: The body is reimagined as viyatvyāpta, pervaded by space, dissolving the sense of compact materiality. The stability of bhāvanā arises not from concentration alone but from repeated recognition that embodied substance is penetrated by the subtle expanse. This is another instance of transforming perceptual objecthood into spatial openness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Undivided Space Within the Body
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
देहान्तरे त्ववविभागम् वभवत्तभूतम् विवचन्तयेत् ।
न वकंवचदन्तरे तस्य ध्यायन्नध्येयभाग्भवेत् ॥ ४८ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantraṃ
dehāntare tva-vibhāgaṃ bhūtabhūtaṃ vicintayet |
na kiñcidantare tasya dhyāyan dhyeyabhāgbhavet || 48 ||
translation: Within the body, one should contemplate the undividedness of the elemental reality of being. Meditating that there is nothing within it, one becomes a participant in the meditated object.
intent_summary: Contemplate the body’s interior as nonseparate and empty of internal divisions until subject and object merge.
beginner_explanation: Look inside the body and imagine that there are no hard boundaries separating things within it. Try not to hunt for anything specific; simply notice absence of separation. When nothing is grasped as an object, the meditator and the meditation can feel like one.
scholar_explanation: Dehāntara here functions as an internal locus for bhūtabhūta, the elemental reality underlying the body, yet its true instruction is to find na kiñcid antaḥ, nothing inside in the ordinary objectifying sense. Dhyeyabhāgbhūta suggests a collapse of the divide between meditator and object of meditation. The verse thus points to nondual absorption through interior negation rather than analytic inquiry.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Heart-Space Absorption
sanskrit:
हृद्याकाशे वनलीनाक्ष् पिसम्पुटमध्यग् ।
अनन्यचेता् सुभगे परं सौभावयमाप्नुयात् ॥ ४९ ॥
transliteration:
hṛdyākāśe nilīnākṣaḥ prasampuṭamadhyagaḥ |
ananyacetāḥ subhage paraṃ saubhāgyam āpnuyāt || 49 ||
translation: With the eyes immersed in the space of the heart and abiding in the middle of the closed palms, one-pointed and unothered, O beautiful one, one attains supreme blessedness.
intent_summary: Withdraw the senses into the heart-space and rest in a sealed, inwardly focused stillness to experience supreme auspiciousness.
beginner_explanation: Imagine your attention sinking into the space of the heart while your hands form a closed, protective enclosure. Keep your awareness simple and undistracted. In that inward stillness, a deep sense of well-being may arise.
scholar_explanation: The verse merges hṛdyākāśa, inner heart-space, with prasampuṭa, the closed/encased palms, creating a contemplative seal. Nilīnākṣaḥ indicates sensory withdrawal, while ananyacetas preserves the nondual focus essential to saubhāgya, auspicious fulfillment. This is an embodied interiorization practice, akin to pratyāhāra but framed within tantric recognition.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Abiding at the Twelfth End
sanskrit:
सिधत् स्वशरीरस्य द्वादशान्ते मनोलयात् ।
दृढिुद्धेदृधढीभूतं तत्त्वलक्ष्यं प्रितधते ॥ ५० ॥
transliteration:
siddhaḥ svazarīrasya dvādaśānte manolayāt |
dṛḍhabuddher dṛḍhībhūtaṃ tattvalakṣyaṃ pravartate || 50 ||
translation: For the perfected one, through the dissolution of mind at the twelfth end of one’s own body, the aim of reality becomes firmly established for the steadfast intellect.
intent_summary: Use the dissolution of mind at the body’s twelfth-point center to stabilize direct realization of truth.
beginner_explanation: There are subtle points beyond the ordinary body where attention can gather and then quiet down. Rest awareness there until thinking subsides. When the mind becomes still, understanding becomes clear and solid.
scholar_explanation: The dvādaśānta, the “twelfth end,” is a subtle locus often associated with cranial or transpersonal apertures in tantric physiology. Through manolaya, the mind dissolves and tattvalakṣya, the target of reality, becomes dṛḍhībhūta, firmly established in dṛḍhabuddhi. The verse combines spatial subtle-body doctrine with the nondual goal of stabilization rather than mere experience.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Attention at the Twelve-Finger Point
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
यथा तथा यि ति द्वादशान्ते मन् वक्षपेत् ॥
प्रवतक्षणम् क्षीणिृत्तेिैलक्षण्यं वदनैभधिेत् ॥ ५१ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantram |
yathā tathā y ti dvādaśānte man vakṣapet ||
pravata-kṣaṇam kṣīṇiṛttailaikṣaṇyaṃ vadanaibhadhiet || 51 ||
translation:
The Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra.
In whatever way one may place the mind at the dvādaśānta, at the end of the twelve-finger span, one should observe the distinctness when mental fluctuations have become exhausted, moment by moment. || 51 ||
intent_summary: Place attention in the subtle end-point of the breath field and notice the mind become distinct and still.
beginner_explanation:
This verse points to a subtle spot beyond the body, often understood as the point where breath and awareness meet. Instead of trying to force anything, you simply rest attention there and watch the mind quiet down.
It is like noticing a distant horizon: the more steadily you look, the less the mind darts around.
scholar_explanation: The practice centers on dvādaśānta, the inner or outer terminus associated with prāṇa and apāna. By fixing manas there, the vṛttis become kṣīṇa and the practitioner apprehends a liṅgatva or distinctive lucidity beyond discursive mentation. This belongs to the breath-and-awareness interface typical of VBT techniques.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Burning the City of Time
sanskrit:
कालाविना कालपदादुवत्थतेन स्वकं पुरम् ।
प्लुष्टं विवचन्तयेदन्ते शान्ताभासस्तदा भिेत् ॥ ५२ ॥
transliteration:
kālāvinā kālapadād utthitena svakaṃ puram |
pluṣṭaṃ vicintayed ante śāntābhāsas tadā bhavet || 52 ||
translation: By the fire of time, arisen from the place of time, one should contemplate one's own city as burned up; then there arises an appearance of peace. || 52 ||
intent_summary: Visualize the entire personal world as consumed and see the calm that appears when attachment to time collapses.
beginner_explanation:
Here you imagine your life and inner world as if they have been burned away by a great fire. This is not about despair; it is about seeing how temporary everything is.
When that grip loosens, a quiet and spacious feeling can appear naturally.
scholar_explanation: The image of svakaṃ puraṃ, the embodied psychic city, being pluṣṭam by kālāgni dissolves identification with temporal succession. The resulting śāntābhāsa is a tranquil resonance or appearance, not yet final liberation but a doorway into disidentification from kāla and its products. The verse uses classical apocalyptic visualization to induce vairāgya and absorption.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Seeing the World as One
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
एवं एव जगत्सं द्विधं ध्यात्वा विकल्पतः ।
अनन्यचेतस् पुम्स् पुम्भाव् परमो भवेत् ॥ ५३ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantram |
evaṃ eva jagatsaṃ dvidhā dhyātvā vikalpataḥ |
ananyacetās puṃs puṃbhāvaḥ paramo bhavet || 53 ||
translation:
The Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra.
Thus, having contemplated the world as divided in two through conceptual construction, the person whose mind is not elsewhere becomes supreme manhood, the highest state. || 53 ||
intent_summary: Recognize that duality is a conceptual overlay and return to undivided awareness.
beginner_explanation:
This verse asks you to notice that the world seems split into many opposites because of thought. If you can see that splitting as something the mind adds, you can relax into a deeper wholeness.
The result is not a better opinion but a stronger sense of being fully present and undivided.
scholar_explanation: The verse targets vikalpa, the conceptual bifurcation that produces apparent duality in jagat. Ananyacetās indicates unwavering, non-distracted consciousness, and puṃbhāva here suggests not gender but the perfected, sovereign condition of a realized person. The teaching aligns with VBT’s recurring insistence that duality is a mentation-induced appearance superimposed on Bhairava-consciousness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Dissolving Subtle Tattvas
sanskrit:
स्वदेहे जगतो वापि सूक्ष्मसूक्ष्मतराणि च ।
तत्त्वानि यानि विलयं ध्यात्वान्ते व्यज्यते परा ॥ ५४ ॥
transliteration:
svadehe jagato vāpi sūkṣma-sūkṣmatarāṇi ca |
tattvāni yāni vilayaṃ dhyātvānte vyajyate parā || 54 ||
translation: In one's own body, or in the world as well, one should contemplate the subtlest of the subtle principles as dissolving; at the end, the supreme appears. || 54 ||
intent_summary: Contemplate all constituent principles as dissolving back into their source so that higher awareness can emerge.
beginner_explanation:
This verse invites you to look at the parts that make up your experience—body, thoughts, and world—and imagine them melting back into something deeper. It is like taking apart a machine to see that it is built from temporary pieces.
When the pieces are seen as unstable, a more basic awareness can shine through.
scholar_explanation: The instruction applies to tattvas in either deha or jagat, emphasizing their progressive subtilization and eventual vilaya. As the practitioner traces phenomena to their finest constituents and lets them dissolve, parā manifests—an immediate recognition of the transcendent Śiva principle. This is a classic tantric inversion of ontological analysis into contemplative deconstruction.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Entering the Heart through the Twelve Gates
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
पीनां च दुिधलां शविं ध्यात्वा द्वादशगोचरे ।
प्रविश्य हृदये ध्यायन्मुि् स्वातन्त्र्यमाप्नुयात् ॥ ५५ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantram |
pīnāṃ ca duidhalāṃ śaktiṃ dhyātvā dvādaśagocare |
praviśya hṛdaye dhyāyan muktiḥ svātantryam āpnuyāt || 55 ||
translation:
The Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra.
Having contemplated the dense, twofold शक्ति (śakti) in the domain of the twelve, and entering into the heart, one who meditates attains liberation and freedom. || 55 ||
intent_summary: Use the body’s subtle channels and the heart-center to enter inwardly and realize freedom.
beginner_explanation:
This verse suggests working with the living energy in the body, especially in relation to the “twelve” subtle openings or spheres. By turning inward to the heart instead of staying scattered outside, you can discover a deeper freedom.
It is like closing the doors of a busy house and going to the quiet center room.
scholar_explanation: The pīnāṃ duidhalāṃ śaktiṃ may point to the dual polarities of embodied energy within the dvādaśa-gocara, the field of twelve. Entering hṛdaya, the central locus of consciousness in Śaiva tantrism, converts energetic contemplation into mukti and svātantrya, the sovereign freedom of Bhairava. The verse foregrounds embodiment as a gateway rather than an obstacle.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Traversing the Cosmic Path
sanskrit:
भुिनार्ध्वावदरूपेण वचन्तयेत्क्रमशोऽवखलम् ।
स्थूलसूक्ष्मपरवस्थत्या यािदन्ते मनोलय् ॥ ५६ ॥
transliteration:
bhuvanārdhva-ādirūpeṇa vicintayet kramaśo'khilam |
sthūla-sūkṣma-para-sthityā yāvad ante manolayaḥ || 56 ||
translation: One should contemplate the entire universe, step by step, in the form of the levels beginning with bhuvana and ārdhva, through gross, subtle, and supreme states, until in the end there is dissolution of mind. || 56 ||
intent_summary: Move contemplation through the layered cosmos until the mind dissolves into stillness.
beginner_explanation:
Think of reality as having layers, from dense and ordinary to subtle and vast. This practice asks you to mentally pass through those layers one by one.
As you do, the mind eventually gets tired of holding onto forms and becomes quiet.
scholar_explanation: The sequence bhuvana-ārdhva suggests a cosmological ascent through graded levels of manifestation, then beyond them. By contemplating sthūla, sūkṣma, and para-sthiti in order, the practitioner allows manolaya to arise organically, echoing VBT’s repeated use of ordered phenomenological ascent. The verse is spatial-cosmological, but the endpoint is psychical absorption.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Contemplating the Lord of the Universe
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरि तन्त्रम्
अस्य सिधस्य विश्वस्य पयधन्तेषु समन्तत् ।
अर्ध्वप्रवक्रयया तत्त्वं शैिं ध्यत्वा महोदय् ॥ ५७ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantram |
asya siddhasya viśvasya paryanteṣu samantataḥ |
adhva-prakriyayā tattvaṃ śaivaṃ dhyātvā mahodaye || 57 ||
translation:
The Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra.
At the limits of this accomplished universe, all around, by the method of the path (adhva), having contemplated the Śaiva principle, one arrives at great awakening. || 57 ||
intent_summary: Perceive the whole cosmos as pervaded by the Śaiva principle and awaken into it.
beginner_explanation:
This verse says that the world is already complete and alive with a deeper presence. You are asked to contemplate that underlying reality everywhere, especially at the edges and boundaries of experience.
When you see the same presence in all directions, a bigger kind of waking up can happen.
scholar_explanation: The siddha-viśva is the perfected universe, and the adhva-prakriyā is the tantric method of tracing the path of manifestation back to Śiva-tattva. Contemplating this principle at the paryanta, the peripheries of experience, generates mahodaya, a great rise or awakening. The verse integrates cosmology with soteriology in a recognizably Trika manner.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Seeing the World as Emptiness
sanskrit:
विश्वमेतन्महादेवि शून्यभूतं विवचन्तयेत् ।
तिैि च मनो लीनं ततस्तल्लयभाजनम् ॥ ५८ ॥
transliteration:
viśvam etan mahādevi śūnyabhūtaṃ vicintayet |
tatraiva ca mano līnaṃ tatas tallayabhājanam || 58 ||
translation: O Great Goddess, one should contemplate this universe as having become empty; there, the mind becomes dissolved, and then one becomes a recipient of that dissolution. || 58 ||
intent_summary: Perceive the world as empty so that mind dissolves into spacious stillness.
beginner_explanation:
You are invited to look at the world and see it as open space rather than as fixed, solid things. When you do, the mind has less to cling to and can sink into that openness.
It is similar to noticing that the screen is untouched by the movie playing on it.
scholar_explanation: Śūnyabhūtaṃ does not mean nihilism but the experiential emptiness of phenomena when seen without inherent solidity. Mano līnaṃ and tallayabhājanaṃ describe the dissolution of mental activity into the very openness it apprehends, a key VBT move from objectification to absorption. This verse closely aligns with śūnya practices elsewhere in Śaiva and Buddhist contemplative idioms, though framed here in Bhairava terms.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Dropping the Wall of Perception
sanskrit:
घटावदभाजने दृवष्टं वभवत्तस्त्यक्त्वा विवनवक्षपेत् ।
तल्लयं तत्क्षणाद्गत्वा तल्लयात्तन्मयो भिेत् ॥ ५९ ॥
transliteration:
ghaṭādiva bhājane dṛṣṭiṃ bhittas tyaktvā vinikṣipet |
tallayaṃ tatkṣaṇād gatvā tallayāt tanmayo bhavet || 59 ||
translation: In a vessel-like receptacle, after abandoning the wall, one should cast the gaze; having gone instantly into that dissolution, one becomes one with that dissolution. || 59 ||
intent_summary: Remove the sense of a boundary or wall and let perception merge instantly into openness.
beginner_explanation:
Imagine looking at space inside a pot or room and no longer paying attention to the wall, only the openness. The verse says that when the boundary is dropped, the mind can merge into that openness immediately.
It is a simple way to shift from seeing objects to resting in the space around them.
scholar_explanation: The ghaṭa imagery works as a classic analogy for bounded cognition: the wall is the conceptual limit, while the inner space is the field of awareness. By tyaktvā bhittiṃ and allowing dṛṣṭi to settle into the receptacle, the practitioner experiences tatkṣaṇa-laya and becomes tanmaya, identified with that dissolution itself. This is a refined visual-spatial technique leading from perception to absorption.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Gaze into the Unbroken Space
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरि तन्त्रम्
वनिृधक्षवगवरवभत्त्यावददेशे दृवष्टं विवनवक्षपेत् ।
विलीने मानसे भािे िृत्तिक्षीण् प्रजायते ॥ ६० ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantram |
vidhṛkṣavigraha-bhittyādi-deśe dṛṣṭiṃ vinikṣipet |
vilīne mānase bhāve vṛtti-kṣīṇāḥ prajāyate || 60 ||
translation:
The Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra.
One should cast the gaze into a place free of walls, bodies, and partitions; when the mental state has dissolved, the mental movements are exhausted. || 60 ||
intent_summary: Rest attention in an unbroken open place until mental activity subsides.
beginner_explanation:
This verse asks you to look into a place with no obvious barriers—like open sky or an uncluttered expanse. Instead of focusing on objects, let your attention rest in openness itself.
When the mind relaxes into that openness, thoughts begin to thin out on their own.
scholar_explanation: The instruction to place dṛṣṭi in a deśa devoid of bhitti and vigraha directs attention away from segmentation toward open awareness. With vilīna-mānasa-bhāva, the affective-cognitive state dissolves, and vṛtti-kṣaya follows naturally. This is one of VBT’s classic śūnya-like contemplations, emphasizing de-centered seeing over object-focused meditation.

speaker: Bhairava
title: The Middle Between Two
sanskrit:
उभयोभाधियोज्ञाधने ध्यात्वा मध्यं समाश्रयेत् ।
युगपच्च द्वयं त्यक्त्वा मध्ये तत्त्वं प्रकाशते ॥ ६१ ॥
transliteration:
ubhayorbhādhiyojñādhaune dhyātvā madhyaṃ samāśrayet |
yugapac ca dvayaṃ tyaktvā madhye tattvaṃ prakāśate || 61 ||
translation: Meditating on the middle between the two, one should take refuge in the center. By abandoning both together, the reality shines forth in the middle.
intent_summary: Focus awareness on the interval between opposites and let both sides drop away so the underlying reality can reveal itself.
beginner_explanation: This verse points you to the quiet gap between two things, like the pause between two breaths or the space between two thoughts. Instead of choosing one side, rest in the middle where neither side is dominating. In that gap, the mind can become very still and clearer awareness can appear.
scholar_explanation: This is a classic madhya-upāya: realization arises in the interval (madhya) between polarities, where dualistic division is suspended. The instruction to abandon both simultaneously suggests a non-conceptual resting beyond paired opposites, not merely balancing them. It echoes VBT techniques centered on sandhi and the middle point as the locus of prakāśa.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Dropping All Objects
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
भावे त्यक्ते निरुद्धा चित्तं नैव भावान्तरं व्रजेत् ।
तदा तन्मध्यभावेन विकसत्यतिभावना ॥ ६२ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantram
bhāve tyakte niruddhaṃ cittaṃ naiva bhāvāntaraṃ vrajet |
tadā tanmadhyabhāvena vikasatyatibhāvanā || 62 ||
translation: When an object or condition is relinquished, and the mind is restrained so that it does not move toward another object, then, by that middle condition, extraordinary contemplation unfolds.
intent_summary: Release one mental content and prevent the mind from rushing to the next, allowing a deeper contemplative openness to expand.
beginner_explanation: Usually the mind jumps from one thing to another. This verse says: let one thought, feeling, or object fall away, and do not immediately replace it with something else. If you can stay in that brief open space, awareness becomes more vivid and expansive.
scholar_explanation: The practice is bhāva-tyāga with cittanirodha in the transition before a new bhāva arises. The phrase tanmadhyabhāvena indicates that the liminal state itself becomes the support for ati-bhāvanā, a heightened contemplative intensity. This is closely related to other VBT methods that use cessation and the gap between mental formations.

speaker: Bhairava
title: World as Conscious Body
sanskrit:
सिं देहं चिन्मयं हि जगद्वा परिभावयेत् ।
युगपन्निविधकल्पेन मनसा परमोदयः ॥ ६३ ॥
transliteration:
sinha dehaṃ cinmayaṃ hi jagadvā paribhāvayet |
yugapan nividhakalpena manasā paramodayaḥ || 63 ||
translation: One should regard the body as made of consciousness, or else the world likewise, with a mind that conceives both together in various ways; supreme arising occurs.
intent_summary: See either the body or the whole world as nothing other than consciousness, until that insight blossoms into awakening.
beginner_explanation: This verse asks you to look at your body, or even the whole world, as if it were made of awareness itself. It is like seeing a wave and realizing it is only water. Holding that vision can open into a bigger sense of yourself and everything around you.
scholar_explanation: Here deha and jagat are re-envisioned as cinmaya, made of consciousness, dissolving the split between perceiver and perceived. The verse permits multiple formulations (nividhakalpena), suggesting flexible contemplative reappraisal rather than fixed imagery. The result is paramodaya, the supreme arising of recognition (pratyabhijñā) of one’s own nature.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Junction of Breath Currents
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरि तन्त्रम्
िायुद्वयस्य सम्घट्टाद् अन्तर् िा िवहरन्तत् ।
योगी समत्वविज्ञानसमुद्गमनभाजनम् ॥ ६४ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantram
vāyudvayasya saṃghaṭṭād antar vā viharantat |
yogī samatvavijñānasamudgamanabhājanam || 64 ||
translation: From the collision or meeting of the two breaths, inwardly or in their movement, the yogī becomes the vessel for the arising of knowledge of equality (samatva).
intent_summary: Attend to the point where the two breath currents meet so that a balanced, unified awareness can arise.
beginner_explanation: Breathing has a natural rhythm, and this verse points to the place where the in-breath and out-breath meet or touch. If you pay attention there, the breath can quiet down and the mind can feel more even. That evenness can support a deeper sense of peace and balance.
scholar_explanation: The verse invokes vāyudvaya-saṃghaṭṭa, the junction of prāṇa and apāna or inhalation and exhalation, as a doorway to samatva-jñāna. The yogī becomes a pātra, a receptacle, for the emergence of equanimous gnosis, a frequent VBT strategy of using breath-sandhi as a portal to awareness.
