Despite OCR noise, the doctrinal thrust is clearly prāṇic transition as a contemplative support.

speaker: Bhairava
title: World as One's Own Bliss
sanskrit:
सिं जगत्स्वदेहं िा स्वानन्दभवरतं स्मरेत् ।
युगपत्स्वामृतेनैि परानन्दमयो भिेत् ॥ ६५ ॥
transliteration:
sinha jagat svadehaṃ vā svānandabharaṃ smaret |
yugapatsvāmṛtenaiva parānandamayo bhavet || 65 ||
translation: One should remember the world, or one's own body, as filled with one's own bliss. At once, by one's own nectar, one becomes made of supreme bliss.
intent_summary: Saturate perception with the feeling that all experience is your own blissful nature, until that bliss becomes total.
beginner_explanation: Instead of seeing the world as cold or separate, this verse invites you to feel it as warm, intimate, and full of your own joy. You can imagine your body and the world itself as overflowing with delight. When that feeling becomes complete, it can turn into a deep and steady happiness.
scholar_explanation: The practice reinterprets jagat or deha as svānanda-bhara, filled with one’s own innate bliss, aligning affect with nondual recognition. Through smṛti and immediate immersion in svāmṛta, the practitioner becomes parānandamaya, constituted by transcendent bliss. This is an emotion-based upāya that transforms aesthetic or devotional delight into contemplative realization.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Delight Through Surprise
sanskrit:
कुहनेन प्रयोगेण सद्य एि मृगेक्षणे ।
समुदेवत महानन्दो येन तत्त्वम् प्रकाशते ॥ ६६ ॥
transliteration:
kuhanena prayogeṇa sadya eva mṛgīkṣaṇe |
samuddevata mahānando yena tattvam prakāśate || 66 ||
translation: By a subtle or mysterious practice, O gazelle-eyed one, immediately there arises great joy through which the truth becomes manifest.
intent_summary: Use a surprising or ingenious contemplative method to generate a sudden joy that unveils reality.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that sometimes awakening comes through an unexpected, almost playful method. A sudden shift can bring a burst of joy, like seeing something beautiful and being momentarily stunned. In that freshness, deeper truth can become visible.
scholar_explanation: The term kuhanā suggests an artful, subtle, or perhaps enigmatic technique that produces immediate mahānanda. This is not ordinary pleasure but an upsurge of transformed affect that reveals tattva. The verse reflects the VBT tendency to exploit emotional surprise and heightened receptivity as a direct route to recognition.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Ascending by Breath Focus
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
सिधस्रोतोवनिन्धेन प्राणशक्त्योर्ध्वधया शनैः ।
वपपीलस्पशधिेलायां प्रथते परमं सुखम् ॥ ६७ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantram
sahasrasrotonibandhena prāṇaśaktyordhvadhayā śanaiḥ |
pipīlaspṛśavelāyāṃ prathate paramaṃ sukham || 67 ||
translation: By gently directing the upward movement of the power of breath through the binding of the thousand channels, at the moment of ant-hill-like touch, supreme bliss unfolds.
intent_summary: Guide subtle breath energy upward with delicate attention until a very fine sensory threshold opens into bliss.
beginner_explanation: This verse uses the image of very subtle attention to the breath moving upward through the body. You do not force anything; you simply guide and feel the energy gently. At a tiny, almost ticklish threshold of sensation, a deep happiness can appear.
scholar_explanation: The image of sahasrasrota is likely the network of channels culminating in the sahasrāra, while prāṇaśakti is led ūrdhva-dhā. The pipīlaspṛśa-velā, a moment of ant-like touch, indicates an extremely subtle sensory threshold where ordinary perception gives way to parama-sukha. This is a refined prāṇic and somatic dhāraṇā linking subtle ascent with tactile liminality.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Fill the Void with Breath
sanskrit:
िह्नेविधषस्य मध्ये तु वचत्तं सुखमयं वक्षपेत् ।
केिलं िायुपूणं िा स्मरानन्देन युज्यते ॥ ६८ ॥
transliteration:
vahnevṛddhasya madhye tu cittaṃ sukhamayaṃ kṣipet |
kevalaṃ vāyupūrṇaṃ vā smarānandena yujyate || 68 ||
translation: In the middle of the growing fire, one should cast the mind, made of happiness. Or one may simply be filled with air and united with the bliss of remembrance.
intent_summary: Place the mind into the energetic center and let breath-filled awareness merge with blissful recollection.
beginner_explanation: Here the practice is to rest the mind in the midst of rising inner heat or intensity. Another option is simply to become full of breath and stay there with a feeling of remembrance. Either way, the point is to let the mind settle into a pleasant inner fullness.
scholar_explanation: The verse places citta in the madhya of the increasing vahni, likely inner heat or transformative energy, yielding sukhamaya absorption. Alternatively, being vāyupūrṇa suggests a balanced, breath-filled state suffused with smara-ānanda, the joy of contemplative recollection. This bridges prāṇa, inner fire, and blissful memory as supports for samādhi.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Bliss in Union
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरि तन्त्रम्
शविसंगमसंक्षुब्धशक्त्यािेशािसावनकम् ।
यत्सुखम् ब्रह्मतत्त्वस्य तत्सुखम् स्वाक्यमुच्यते ॥ ६९ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantram
śaktisaṃgama-saṃkṣubdha-śaktyāveśāvasānikam |
yat sukham brahmatattvasya tat sukham svākhyam ucyate || 69 ||
translation: The bliss that belongs to Brahman-reality, ending in the entry of power stirred by the union of Śakti, is called one's own bliss.
intent_summary: Recognize the bliss arising from the union and stirring of śakti as your own deepest nature, not something external.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that the deepest joy is not borrowed from outside—it is your own nature. When energy, love, or inner power becomes fully awakened, it can feel like a powerful union. That experience points back to the absolute bliss of reality itself.
scholar_explanation: Śaktisaṃgama and śaktyāveśa indicate the activation of consciousness-power through union, whether literal or interiorized. The resulting sukha is identified with brahmatattva and explicitly named svākhya, one’s own innate bliss, reinforcing the nondual identity of the practitioner with ultimate reality. The verse aligns tantric energy with ontological recognition rather than merely erotic symbolism.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Erotic Bliss as Awareness
sanskrit:
लेहनामन्थनाकोटै् स्त्रीसुखस्य भरात्स्मृते् ।
शक्त्यभािेऽवप देिेवश भिेदानन्दसम्प्लि् ॥ ७० ॥
transliteration:
lehanāmanthanakoṭaiḥ strīsukhasya bharāt smṛteḥ |
śaktyabhāve'pi deveśi bhaved ānandasamplavaḥ || 70 ||
translation: Through the stirring, churning, and embrace of the delight of a woman, by the force of recollection, O Lord of the gods, even in the absence of the power, there can arise a flood of bliss.
intent_summary: Use remembrance of intense embodied pleasure to open into bliss that can continue even when the physical stimulus is absent.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that powerful pleasure can be remembered so vividly that bliss can arise even after the moment has passed. It is like the afterglow of a beautiful experience continuing in the mind and body. The practice is to use that remembered intensity as a doorway to deeper happiness.
scholar_explanation: The verse uses explicit erotic imagery—lehanā, manthana, koṭa—to indicate the intensity of embodied sukha and its contemplative transmutation through smṛti. Even when śakti is absent, ānanda-samplava can arise, suggesting that the inner trace of experience becomes a meditative support. This is consistent with VBT’s broader use of heightened affect to reveal nondual delight.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Bliss Absorption
sanskrit:
आनन्दे महवत प्राप्ते दृष्टे िा िान्धिे वचरात् ।
आनन्दमुद्गतम् ध्यात्वा तल्लयस्तन्मना भिेत् ॥ ७१ ॥
transliteration:
ānande mahati prāpte dṛṣṭe vā bāndhave cirāt |
ānandamudgataṃ dhyātvā tallayastanmanā bhavet || 71 ||
translation: When great bliss arises, or when seeing a dear one after a long time, meditate on the rising of that bliss; by merging into it, one becomes identified with that as one's mind.
intent_summary: Use a surge of joy or reunion to enter absorption by resting fully in the felt experience of bliss.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that strong happiness can become a doorway to meditation. Instead of getting lost in the story of why you are happy, simply feel the joy itself and let your attention sink into it. If you do that deeply, the mind naturally quiets down and merges into the experience.
scholar_explanation: This dhāraṇā uses ānanda as an upāya: when intense joy arises—whether from realization or reunion with a bāndhava—the practitioner contemplates the upward surge of bliss and allows laya into that current. The phrase tanmanā bhavet indicates identification through absorption, where subject-object separation thins and ānanda becomes a support for entry into Bhairava-consciousness. It aligns with Tantric methods that convert ordinary affect into nondual access.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Joy of Drinking Elixir
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
जववधपानकृतोल्लासरसानन्दविजृम्भणात् ।
भाियेद्भवरतािस्थां महानन्दस्ततो भिेत् ॥ ७२ ॥
transliteration:
jīvavidhyā-pāna-kṛtollāsa-rasānanda-vijṛmbhaṇāt |
bhāvayed bhairavīṃ avasthāṃ mahānandas tato bhavet || 72 ||
translation: By the overflowing expansion of the rasa of bliss produced by drinking the elixir of the life-teaching, one should contemplate the Bhairavī state; then great bliss arises.
intent_summary: Transform the rapture of inner vitality into contemplation of the divine state until it blossoms as great bliss.
beginner_explanation: This verse points to a heightened inner joy that can feel like being nourished by a divine drink. The instruction is to stay with that wave of delight and contemplate it as a sacred state, not just a passing feeling. When attention settles there, a deeper and larger joy can emerge.
scholar_explanation: The OCR-like jīvavidhyā-pāna likely points to a subtle Tantric elixir-imagery: the induced ullāsa-rasa-ananda is not merely emotional but a sacralized vitality. By bhāvaying bhairavīṃ avasthām, the yogin contemplates the Bhairavī condition, the śakti-side of nondual awareness, from which mahānanda arises. The verse emphasizes aesthetic-rasa transmutation into contemplative realization.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Taste of Detachment
sanskrit:
वगतावदविषयास्वादासमसौख्यैकतात्मन् ।
योवगनस्तन्मयत्वेन मनोरूढेस् तदात्मता ॥ ७३ ॥
transliteration:
gatādi-viṣayāsvāda-sama-saukhyaikatātman |
yoginas tanmayatvena manorūḍhe tadātmatā || 73 ||
translation: For the yogin whose very self is unified with the equal pleasure that comes from the taste of past and future objects, by becoming fully one with that, the mind ascends into that very identity.
intent_summary: Recognize equalized pleasure in experience and let the mind become fully absorbed in it until identity shifts.
beginner_explanation: Here the point is not to chase new pleasures, but to notice a stable, even joy that is less dependent on any one object. If you rest in that feeling long enough, the mind can settle into it and stop scattering outward. It's like soaking in a warm bath until you forget the edges of your body.
scholar_explanation: This verse speaks of sama-saukhya and tanmayatva: a uniform सुख that is not object-dependent in the usual way, but arises when the yogin’s awareness is no longer captivated by discrete viṣaya-asvāda. As manorūḍha, the mind is lifted into tadātmatā, indicating ontological identity through contemplative saturation. The verse thus redirects sense-content into a nondual aesthetic-equanimous absorption.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Rest in Any Satisfaction
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
यि यि मनस्तुवष्टमधनस्तिैि धारयेत् ।
ति ति परानन्दस्वारूपं सम्प्रितधते ॥ ७४ ॥
transliteration:
yatra yatra manastuṣṭir madhustatraiva dhārayet |
tatra tatra parānanda-svarūpaṃ sampratipadyate || 74 ||
translation: Wherever there is satisfaction of the mind, there one should hold firm; there and there the nature of supreme bliss is attained.
intent_summary: Use any genuine satisfaction as an entry point to the recognition of supreme bliss.
beginner_explanation: This verse gives a very practical instruction: whenever you feel truly content, pause and stay there. Don't rush to the next thing. By holding your attention in that simple satisfaction, you may discover a deeper happiness underneath it.
scholar_explanation: The teaching is broad and portable: any instance of manastuṣṭi becomes a dhāraṇā-point. By dhārayet there, the practitioner discovers parānanda-svarūpa, showing that ordinary contentment can reveal the substratum of supreme bliss when not fragmented by desire. This is a classic Tantric inversion of everyday affect into a doorway to the absolute.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Before Sleep into the Goddess
sanskrit:
अनागतायां वनद्रायां प्रणष्टे िाह्यगोचरे ।
सािस्था मनसा गम्या परा देिी प्रकाशते ॥ ७५ ॥
transliteration:
anāgatāyāṃ nidrāyāṃ praṇaṣṭe bāhyagocare |
sāvasthā manasā gamyā parā devī prakāśate || 75 ||
translation: When sleep has not yet arrived and external objects have faded away, that state is accessible to the mind; in it, the supreme Goddess shines forth.
intent_summary: Catch the threshold before sleep and rest awareness there until the Goddess-like presence becomes evident.
beginner_explanation: This verse is about the quiet moment just before falling asleep, when the outside world starts to fade. Instead of following thoughts or drifting off immediately, stay aware of that in-between state. In that stillness, a deeper presence can appear.
scholar_explanation: The dhāraṇā targets the liminal state of anāgatā nidrā, where external viṣaya-gocara has ceased but full sleep has not yet commenced. This twilight of consciousness is accessible to manas and reveals parā devī prakāśate, indicating śakti as luminous awareness prior to conceptualization. The practice exploits the dissolution of sensory fixation into a naturally luminous threshold state.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Sky of Light Gazing
sanskrit:
तेजसा सूयधदीपादेराकाशे शिलीकृते ।
दृवष्टवनधिेश्या तिैि स्वात्मरूपं प्रकाशते ॥ ७६ ॥
transliteration:
tejasā sūryadīpāder ākāśe śakalīkṛte |
dṛṣṭir niveśyā tatraiva svātmarūpaṃ prakāśate || 76 ||
translation: When the sky is made distinct by the radiance of the sun, lamp, and so on, fix the gaze there; there one's own self-form shines forth.
intent_summary: Use luminous space or the bright field of vision as a focus until self-awareness reveals itself.
beginner_explanation: Look at a bright, open space—like sunlight or a lamp-lit area—and rest your gaze there. The point is not to stare hard, but to let the eyes and mind become calm in the light. In that openness, your own inner awareness can become more obvious.
scholar_explanation: This is a visual ālambana in which tejas renders ākāśa as a clarified field, suitable for dṛṣṭi-niveśana. The external luminosity serves as a mirror for svātma-rūpa, indicating that self-luminosity (svaprakāśatā) is recognized through contemplative seeing. The verse joins visualization with awareness, but the decisive emphasis is on the light revealing the seer.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Catching the Gaze of Bhairavi
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
करवङ्कण्या क्रोधनया भैरव्या लेलिहानया ।
खेचयाध दृवष्टकाले च परािावप्त् प्रकाशते ॥ ७७ ॥
transliteration:
karakāṅkāṇyā krodhanayā bhairavyā lelihānayā |
khecaryā dṛṣṭikāle ca parāvāptiḥ prakāśate || 77 ||
translation: By the fierce, eager Bhairavī with her hand-signs and gestures, and at the time of the khecarī gaze, supreme attainment shines forth.
intent_summary: Use the fierce, upward-moving gaze and symbolic gesture of Bhairavī to open into supreme realization.
beginner_explanation: This verse describes a powerful meditation using a lifted, intense gaze and the energy of a fierce goddess form. The practice is not about imagination alone; it is about letting the gaze and inner feeling become very alert and upward-moving. In that heightened state, a deeper realization can break through.
scholar_explanation: The verse invokes Bhairavī in a vivid iconographic mode, with krodhanā and lelihānā suggesting potent, consuming śakti. Khecarī-dṛṣṭi at the moment of gaze is a classic upward internalization of attention, culminating in parāvāpti, the supreme attainment beyond ordinary perception. The glyphic body-gesture and gaze work together as a sacramental concentration on śakti-ascent.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Seated Unsupportedly
sanskrit:
मृद्वासने विजैकेन हस्तपादौ वनराश्रयम् ।
वनधाय तत्प्रसङ्गेन परा पूणाध मवतभधिेत् ॥ ७८ ॥
transliteration:
mṛdvāsane vijānekena hastapādau nirāśrayam |
nidhāya tat-prasaṅgena parā pūrṇā matir bhavet || 78 ||
translation: Seated on a soft seat, place the hands and feet without support, and through that orientation the supreme, पूर्ण, full mind arises.
intent_summary: Adopt a simple unsupported posture so bodily ease can give rise to a full, spacious mind.
beginner_explanation: Sit comfortably and let your hands and feet rest without bracing them. The idea is to remove unnecessary effort from the body so the mind also becomes less tense. When the body is settled in this uncomplicated way, awareness can feel fuller and calmer.
scholar_explanation: This is a body-based upāya using mṛdvāsana and nirāśraya placement of limbs to reduce muscular and psychic contraction. Through that bodily non-support, prasaṅga leads to parā pūrṇā mati, where fullness is not manufactured but revealed. The verse shows how physical ease can quietly disclose the nondual plenum.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Arms Folded into Calm
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
उपविश्यासने सम्यविाहू कृत्वाधधकुवञ्चतौ ।
कक्षव्योवि मन् कुिधन् शममायावत तल्लयात् ॥ ७९ ॥
transliteration:
upaviśyāsane samyag bāhū kṛtvārdhakuñcitau |
kakṣavyomni manāṃ kurvan śamam āyāti tallayāt || 79 ||
translation: Sitting on the seat with the arms properly half-bent, making the mind enter the space of the armpits, one comes to calm through that absorption.
intent_summary: Focus inward on the embodied space around the armpits while maintaining a relaxed seated posture until calm emerges.
beginner_explanation: This verse asks you to sit and gently bend your arms, then notice the small inward space near the armpits. It may sound unusual, but the purpose is to draw attention into the body rather than outward into busy thoughts. As attention stays there, the mind settles down.
scholar_explanation: The practice locates awareness in kakṣa-vyoman, the subtle bodily space of the armpits, while the body is held in a specific but not strained configuration. The inwardness of manas and the sense of enclosure support śama through tallaya, a soft absorption rather than forceful concentration. This is an embodiment practice that uses proprioceptive subtlety to still mental dispersal.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Steady Gaze, Unfixed Mind
sanskrit:
स्थूलरूपस्य भािस्य स्तब्धां दृवष्टं वनपात्य च ।
अवचरेण वनराधारं मन् कृत्वा वशिं व्रजेत् ॥ ८० ॥
transliteration:
sthūlarūpasya bhāvasya stabdhāṃ dṛṣṭiṃ nipātya ca |
acireṇa nirādhāraṃ man kurvan śivaṃ vrajet || 80 ||
translation: Having cast a fixed gaze on a gross form or object, and quickly making the mind unsupported, one goes to Śiva.
intent_summary: Use steady looking at a concrete object, then let the mind drop its support and enter Shiva-nature.
beginner_explanation: First, look steadily at something solid and simple. Then, after a moment, let the mind stop clinging to the object and just become open and unsupported. In that opening, the text says one can move into a deeper state of peace and presence.
scholar_explanation: The sequence is deliberate: dṛṣṭi is stabilized on sthūla-rūpa, then the mental support is withdrawn into nirādhāratā. The contrast between object-fixation and supportless mind reveals śiva, suggesting a transition from gross perception to non-objective awareness. This is a common Tantric movement from form to formlessness without rejecting the form outright.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Tongue-Cavity Inner Mantra
sanskrit:
मध्यवजह्वे िावरतास्ये मध्ये वनक्षप्य चेतनाम् ।
होच्चारं मनसा कुिंस्तत् शान्ते प्रलीयते ॥ ८१ ॥
transliteration: madhyavadvajhe śivaratāsyе madhye nikṣipya cetanām | hoccāraṃ manasā kurvīt tat śānte pralīyate || 81 ||
translation: Placing awareness in the middle, in the tongue-cavity or the mouth-space, one should mentally make the ‘ho’ utterance; when that is calmed, one dissolves.
intent_summary: Use a subtle internal articulation and then let it fade into stillness, so awareness merges into quiet absorption.
beginner_explanation: This verse asks you to focus attention in the middle of the mouth or throat and mentally form a sound, then let it settle. It is like noticing the beginning of a word and then resting in the silence after it. The point is not speaking aloud, but sensing how sound arises and disappears inside awareness.
scholar_explanation: The verse employs an internalized uccāra, here OCR-corrupted as “ho,” as a dhāraṇā on madhya, the central locus. By placing cetanā in the oral center and mentally performing the utterance, the practitioner follows sound back into śānta, where duality collapses into laya. This is akin to other nāda-based upāyas in the VBT that use mantra, resonance, and cessation as a doorway to Bhairava-consciousness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Resting in Unsupported Awareness
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
आसने शयने वस्थत्वा वनराधारं विभाियन् ।
स्वदेहं मनवस वक्षणे क्षणात्क्षीणाशयो भिेत् ॥ ८२ ॥
transliteration: vijñānabhairava tantram | āsane śayane sthitvā nirādhāraṃ vibhāvayan | svadehaṃ manasi kṣaṇe kṣaṇāt kṣīṇāśayo bhavet || 82 ||
translation: In sitting or lying down, contemplating the unsupported, one should place one’s own body in the mind; in a moment, the mind’s tendencies become exhausted.
intent_summary: Contemplate everything as resting on no support, including your own body, until mental habits quickly weaken.
beginner_explanation: This verse says to sit or lie down and imagine your body without any outer support, as if it were floating in awareness. When you hold this view steadily, ordinary worries and habits begin to lose their force. It is a way of loosening the mind by seeing the body as not ultimately solid or separate.
scholar_explanation: The key term nirādhāra indicates a supportless contemplative stance, undoing the mind’s dependence on external and internal substrates. By visualizing svadeha within manas while resting in āsana or śayana, one induces kṣīṇāśaya, the thinning of saṃskāras. The practice resonates with nondual Āgamic methods that reveal the body as a construct within awareness rather than an independent locus of identity.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Stillness Through Gentle Motion
sanskrit:
चलासने वस्थतस्याथ शनैिाध देहचालनात् ।
प्रशान्ते मानसे भािे देवि वदव्यौघम् आप्नुयात् ॥ ८३ ॥
transliteration: calāsane sthitasyātha śanaiḥ deha-cālanāt | praśānte mānase bhāve devi divyaugham āpnuyāt || 83 ||
translation: For one established in a moving posture, by gently moving the body little by little, O Devi, when the mind-state becomes शांत (pacified), one attains a stream of the divine.
intent_summary: Use soft, deliberate bodily movement to calm the mind until a subtle divine flow is felt.
beginner_explanation: If you are fidgety or restless, this verse suggests moving the body slowly instead of forcing stillness. As the movement becomes gentle and your mind relaxes, you can feel a more spacious, peaceful quality emerge. Think of a storm settling into a steady current.
scholar_explanation: Here the method works with calāsana and deha-cālana, using regulated bodily motion as an entry into praśānta mānasa-bhāva. Rather than suppressing kinetic energy, the practitioner refines it until it yields divyaugha, a current of subtle spiritual अनुभूति. This reflects the VBT’s principle that ordinary activity, when fully attended, can dissolve into Bhairava-awareness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Gazing into Clear Space
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरि तन्त्रम्
आकाशं विमलं पश्यन्कृत्वा दृवष्टं वनरन्तराम् ।
स्तब्धात्मा तत्क्षणाद्देवि भैरिं िपुराप्नुयात् ॥ ८४ ॥
transliteration: vijñānabhairava tantram | ākāśaṃ vimalam paśyan kṛtvā dṛṣṭiṃ nirantaram | stabdhātmā tatkṣaṇād devi bhairavaṃ vapur āpnuyāt || 84 ||
translation: Seeing the pure sky or space and making the gaze continuous, with the self held motionless, O Devi, one immediately attains the body of Bhairava.
intent_summary: Fix attention on open, clear space until the mind becomes motionless and Bhairava-consciousness appears.
beginner_explanation: Look into a clear open space, like the sky, without letting your attention jump around. As you keep your gaze steady and your body quiet, your mind can become equally still. The verse says that in that stillness, you directly recognize a vast, Bhairava-like presence.
scholar_explanation: Ākāśa here functions as a visual support for expanding consciousness beyond limited form. Nirantara-dṛṣṭi and stabdhātmā together generate immediacy: the absorption is not gradual but instant, yielding bhairava-vapu, the experiential body of nondual awareness. This dhāraṇā parallels other space contemplations where emptiness is not blankness but luminous openness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Absorbing into the Sky-Centered Bhairava Form
sanskrit:
लीनं मूवनध वियत्सिधम् भैरित्वेन भाियेत् ।
तत्सिधम् भैरिाकारतेजस्तत्त्वं समाविशेत् ॥ ८५ ॥
transliteration: līnaṃ mūrdhni viyat-sarvam bhairavatvena bhāvayet | tat-sarvaṃ bhairavākāra-tejaḥ-tattvaṃ samāviśet || 85 ||
translation: One should contemplate all space, merged in the crown of the head, as Bhairava-hood; then that entire reality enters the luminous principle shaped as Bhairava.
intent_summary: Visualize all of space gathered into the crown and identify it with Bhairava until the whole field of experience is absorbed in that form.
beginner_explanation: Imagine the vast sky or space gathered at the top of your head, like everything opening upward into one bright point. Then let that point be felt as Bhairava, a living presence rather than just an idea. The practice turns openness into a direct experience of sacred awareness.
scholar_explanation: This verse concentrates viyat-sarva in the mūrdhan, the cranial apex, and reinterprets it as bhairavatva. The culmination is samāveśa into bhairavākāra-tejas-tattva, suggesting that the objective cosmos is re-cognized as the radiance of consciousness. It is a classic Tantric inversion: external space is internalized and transmuted into the deity’s own form.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Seeing the World as Bhairava
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरि तन्त्रम्
वकवञ्चज्ज्ञातम् द्वैतदावय बाह्यालोकस्तम् पुन् ।
विश्वावद भैरिं रूपं ज्ञात्वानन्तप्रकाशभृत् ॥ ८६ ॥
transliteration: vijñānabhairava tantram | kiñcijjñātaṃ dvaita-dāyī bāhyāloka-stam punaḥ | viśvādi bhairavaṃ rūpaṃ jñātvānantaprakāśa-bhṛt || 86 ||
translation: Whatever is known in duality, and the outer light that again and again burns it away: knowing the universe and all its beginning as the form of Bhairava, one becomes filled with infinite प्रकाश (light).
intent_summary: See all differentiated experience and even the outer world itself as Bhairava’s form, thereby awakening infinite luminous awareness.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that what we usually take as separate things can be seen differently: as expressions of one reality. Instead of fighting the world, recognize it as the form of Bhairava. When you do, experience becomes bright, spacious, and unified.
scholar_explanation: The line criticizes dvaita, the dualistic stance produced by objectifying cognition, and redirects it toward bhairava-rūpa as the identity of viśva and ādi. Bāhyāloka is not merely external light but the revealing power that can either sustain duality or disclose ananta-prakāśa. The dhāraṇā is ontological re-vision: perception itself becomes a direct recognition of the nondual deity.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Dark Moon Contemplation
sanskrit:
एिमेि दुवनधशायां कृष्णपक्षागमे वचरम् ।
तैवमरं भाियन् रूपं भैरिं रूपमेष्यवत ॥ ८७ ॥
transliteration: evameva duṣṭinśāyāṃ kṛṣṇapakṣāgame ciram | taimiram bhāvayan rūpaṃ bhairavaṃ rūpam eṣyati || 87 ||
translation: In the same way, during the dark fortnight, remaining for a long time, contemplating the dark form, one will attain the form of Bhairava.
intent_summary: Use darkness, night, or the dark lunar phase as a contemplative aid to realize the dark, infinite Bhairava-form.
beginner_explanation: This verse uses the image of the dark moon or night as a meditation support. Instead of fearing darkness, you rest with it and let the mind settle into its depth. The darkness becomes a doorway to a vast, formless presence.
scholar_explanation: Kṛṣṇapakṣa and taimira point to deliberate engagement with darkness as a visual symbol of unmanifest consciousness. Bhairava’s ‘darkness’ is not privation but the fertile obscurity in which forms dissolve back into source. The practice aligns with nocturnal and liminal Tantric contemplations where concealment reveals the absolute.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Closed-Eye Dark Form Meditation
sanskrit:
एिमेि वनमील्यादौ नेिे कृष्णाभमाग्रत् ।
प्रसायध भैरिं रूपं भाियम्स्तन्मयो भिेत् ॥ ८८ ॥
transliteration: evameva nimīlyādau netre kṛṣṇābham agrataḥ | prasārya bhairavaṃ rūpaṃ bhāvayan tanmayo bhavet || 88 ||
translation: In the same way, first closing the eyes, with a dark appearance before one, then expanding, one should contemplate the form of Bhairava; one becomes identified with that.
intent_summary: Close the eyes, attend to the dark field before you, and expand it into Bhairava until your identity merges with it.
beginner_explanation: When you close your eyes, there is usually a dark field in front of you. Watch that darkness, and let it widen instead of trying to see something specific. As you do, the sense of being a separate observer can soften and you may feel united with the vastness you are watching.
scholar_explanation: This dhāraṇā refines visual withdrawal: nimīlya the eyes, one meets kṛṣṇābha, the dark inner field, and then prasāra, expansion, into bhairava-rūpa. The result is tan-maya, ‘made of that,’ a classic term for identity through contemplative assimilation. It is closely related to other śūnya and ākāśa practices but emphasizes the perceptual afterimage of darkness as a portal.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Sense Withdrawal into Emptiness
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरि तन्त्रम्
यस्य कस्येवन्द्रयस्यावप व्याघाताच्च वनरोधत् ।
प्रविष्टस्याद्वये शून्ये तिैिात्मा प्रकाशते ॥ ८९ ॥
transliteration: vijñānabhairava tantram | yasya kasyendriyasyāpi vyāghātāc ca nirodhat | praviṣṭasyādvaye śūnye tathaivātmā prakāśate || 89 ||
translation: By obstructing and restraining any one of the senses, when one has entered the nondual void, then the Self shines forth exactly there.
intent_summary: Interrupt sense activity and let attention sink into nondual emptiness, where the true Self reveals itself.
beginner_explanation: Pick one sense, like hearing or sight, and gently interrupt its usual outward flow. In that brief gap, instead of chasing the next object, rest in the open space that appears. The verse says that this open space is where your true self can be felt most clearly.
scholar_explanation: Nirodha of even a single indriya can open advaya-śūnya, indicating that sensory blockage is used not as suppression but as an aperture into self-luminous awareness. The verse is important for its claim that ātmā prakāśate precisely in the gap created by sense interruption. This is one of the clearest VBT formulations of śūnya as experientially nondual, not nihilistic.

speaker: Bhairava
title: AUM Contemplation Beyond Bindu and Visarga
sanskrit:
अविन्दुम् अविसगधम् च अकारम् जपतो महान् ।
उदेवत देवि सहसा ज्ञानौघ् परमेश्वर् ॥ ९० ॥
transliteration: avindum avisargam ca akāram japato mahān | udeti devi sahasā jñānaughaḥ parameśvaraḥ || 90 ||
translation: For the great one who chants A, without bindu and without visarga, O Devi, the flood of knowledge, the supreme Lord, suddenly arises.
intent_summary: Repeat the sacred syllable A in a purified, subtle way until a sudden wave of direct knowledge arises.
beginner_explanation: This verse focuses on a very simple sound, the ‘A’ of AUM, but stripped of extra markings or elaboration. By holding it clearly and quietly, the sound can open into a sudden insight that feels larger than thought. It is like using one pure note to tune the whole instrument of attention.
scholar_explanation: The instruction isolates akāra while excluding bindu and visarga, pointing to the primordial phoneme as a direct access to parameśvara. The resulting jñānaugha is not discursive knowledge but a spontaneous flood of recognition. In VBT terms, sound here functions as a seed that ripens into immediate nondual revelation.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Spelling Vowel Resonance into the Final Silence
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
वर्णस्य सविसर्गस्य विसर्गान्तं चेतनं कुरु ।
निराधारेण चित्तेन स्पृशेद्ब्रह्म सनातनम् ॥ ९१ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantraṃ
varṇasya savisargasya visargāntaṃ cetanaṃ kuru |
nirādhāreṇa cittena spṛśed brahma sanātanam || 91 ||
translation: Make your awareness the ending of a syllable together with its visarga, and with a supportless mind touch the eternal Brahman.
intent_summary: Use attention on the fading end of sound to enter the silent ground beyond sound.
beginner_explanation: Listen closely to the end of a spoken sound, especially the little fading after it. Then let your attention rest in the silence that remains when the sound disappears. The practice is to notice that silence is not empty in a dead way, but full and steady.
scholar_explanation: This dhāraṇā uses the end of varṇa with visarga as a gateway into the liminal vanishing point of nāda. By holding cit in the visargānta, the practitioner approaches brahma sanātana through nirādhāra-citta, echoing VBT methods that use sonic dissolution to reveal the background of consciousness. It belongs with the text’s sound-based contemplations on śabda and laya.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Meditating the Self as Sky-Like Space
sanskrit:
व्योमाकारं स्वमात्मानम् ध्यायेवद्दवग्भरनािृतम् ।
निराश्रया चित्त् शवि् स्वरूपं दशधयेत्तदा ॥ ९२ ॥
transliteration:
vyomākāraṃ svam ātmānam dhyāyed avagbharaṇāvṛtam |
nirāśrayā cittiśaktiḥ svarūpaṃ darśayed tadā || 92 ||
translation: One should meditate on one’s own Self as having the form of space, filled with and covered by the weight of speech; then the supportless power of mind reveals its own nature.
intent_summary: Contemplate the self as vast space so that mind, freed from supports, discloses its true form.
beginner_explanation: Imagine your own self not as a small body, but as open space with no edges. Let thoughts and words feel like clouds passing through that space. When you stop clinging to anything solid, a wider, freer sense of being can appear.
scholar_explanation: The verse identifies ātmā with vyomākāra, suggesting an ākāśa-like consciousness in which vāk and mental formations are superimposed. When cittiśakti becomes nirāśrayā, it reveals svarūpa; this resonates with VBT contemplations that shift identity from bounded body-mind to the vastness of cit/ākāśa. The OCR is unstable, but the practical direction remains a visualization of infinite openness leading to self-recognition.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Splitting the Body with Needlelike Attention
sanskrit:
किंचिदङ्गम् विभिद्यादौ तीक्ष्णसूच्यावदना तत् ।
तथैव चेतनां युक्त्वा भैरवे निर्मला गतिः ॥ ९३ ॥
transliteration:
kiñcid aṅgaṃ vibhidya ādyau tīkṣṇa-sūcyāvadānaṃ tat |
tathaiva cetanāṃ yuktvā bhairave nirmalā gatiḥ || 93 ||
translation: Pierce some part of the body at the outset with a sharp needle-like focus; in the same way, by joining awareness there, there is a pure movement into Bhairava.
intent_summary: Use intense, precise bodily attention at one point to enter a clear nondual state.
beginner_explanation: Pick a small spot in the body and focus on it as if a tiny needle were touching it. Don’t imagine much—just stay precise and steady. By doing this, attention can become so concentrated that ordinary mental chatter drops away.
scholar_explanation: This is a bodily dhāraṇā using avadhāna-like precision, where a localized bodily point becomes the support for concentrated awareness. The sharpness of tīkṣṇa-sūci evokes the cutting through of dispersion and the unification of cetanā with the locus of sensation, producing nirmalā gati into Bhairava. It parallels VBT tactile and somatic techniques that transform embodied sensation into a door to nonduality.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Perceiving the Mind's Ends Through Nonconceptuality
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
वचत्ताद्यन्त्कृवतनाधवस्त ममान्तभाधियेवदवत ।
विकल्पानामभािेन विकल्पैरुवितो भिेत् ॥ ९४ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantraṃ
cittādyanta-kṛti-nātha vastv amāntabhāri eva iti |
vikalpānām abhāvena vikalpair udito bhavet || 94 ||
translation: By the absence of mental constructions, one may become established in what is prior to mind and end; thus one becomes arisen through thought-forms without thought-forms.
intent_summary: See beyond conceptual constructions by noticing the source from which thoughts arise and into which they end.
beginner_explanation: Watch how thoughts start and stop, but don’t get caught in the stories they tell. Try to sense the place before a thought appears and after it fades. The verse points to a freedom that is there even while thoughts come and go.
scholar_explanation: The verse points to the nondual ground that is prior to citta and its anta, using the paradox of vikalpa-s only to transcend vikalpa. The wording suggests that by the very absence of conceptual fixation, the practitioner abides in the unconstructed source, consistent with VBT’s apophatic route to Bhairava. It aligns with practices of witnessing the arising and ending of mental movement without appropriation.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Seeing Through Māyā as Pure Determination
sanskrit:
माया विमोवहनी नाम कलाया् कलनं वस्थतम् ।
इत्यावदधमं तत्त्वानां कलयन्न पृथग्भिेत् ॥ ९५ ॥
transliteration:
māyā vimohinī nāma kalāyāḥ kalanaṃ sthitam |
ityādi-dharmān tattvānāṃ kalayan na pṛthag bhavet || 95 ||
translation: Māyā, the deluder, is established as the delimitation of kalā; by discerning the characteristics beginning with this and the other principles of reality, one does not become separate.
intent_summary: Recognize māyā and the tattvas without reifying them, so they no longer divide experience into separate realities.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that the world’s divisions are made by subtle acts of measuring and labeling. Instead of fighting those divisions, just see them clearly as movements of mind and energy. Then they stop feeling like absolute barriers.
scholar_explanation: Here māyā is identified with kalā as the principle of limitation and individuation within the tattva scheme. By ‘kalayan’—discriminating the tattvas while not taking them as separate—the practitioner avoids reification and remains in nondual awareness despite the play of cosmic categories. This fits the VBT tendency to use doctrinal analysis as a means of deconstructing separative cognition.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Calming a Sudden Desire as It Arises
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरि तन्त्रम्
झवगतीच्छां समुत्पन्नामिलोक्य शमं नयेत् ।
यत एि समुद्भूता ततस्तिैि लीयते ॥ ९६ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantraṃ
jhaṭitīcchāṃ samutpannām avalokya śamaṃ nayet |
yata eva samudbhūtā tatas taiva līyate || 96 ||
translation: Seeing a desire that has suddenly arisen, one should bring it to stillness; for from whatever it has arisen, in that very source it dissolves.
intent_summary: Observe desire the moment it appears and let it subside back into its source.
beginner_explanation: When a strong desire suddenly shows up, don’t immediately act on it. Just notice it clearly and let it settle on its own. Like a wave falling back into the sea, the desire can dissolve if you stop feeding it.
scholar_explanation: The verse uses the jhaṭitīcchā as an immediate object for śama, transforming reactive desire into a contemplative doorway. Since the desire originates from the same source into which it dissolves, the practitioner directly sees its dependent arising and fading, which supports recognition of the underlying awareness. This is a classic VBT move: use affective energy itself as the means of return.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Abiding Where Desire and Knowledge Do Not Arise
sanskrit:
यदा ममेच्छा नोत्पन्ना ज्ञानं िा कस्तदावस्म िै ।
तत्त्वतोऽहम् तथाभूतस्तल्लीनस्तन्मना भिेत् ॥ ९७ ॥
transliteration:
yadā mamecchā notpannā jñānaṃ vā kas tadā asmi vai |
tattvato 'ham tathābhūtas tallīnas tanmanā bhavet || 97 ||
translation: When my desire has not arisen, nor knowledge—what am I then? Truly, I am of that nature; one should become absorbed in that and have one’s mind on that.
intent_summary: Rest in the state where no desire or cognition has yet formed, and merge attention into that pure being.
beginner_explanation: Ask yourself what is present before any urge or thought shows up. Don’t try to answer with words; just rest in that open, simple presence. The point is to notice that your deepest identity is there even before thinking begins.
scholar_explanation: This verse uses a contemplative self-query to locate the state prior to icchā and jñāna, effectively pointing to bare being as the practitioner’s identity. The phrase tathābhūta emphasizes abiding as ‘that which is thus,’ and tallīna/tanmanā indicate absorption of mind into that unconditioned presence. It closely supports the VBT’s use of preconceptual awareness as a direct route to Bhairava.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Placing the Mind in Desire or Knowledge
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरि तन्त्रम्
इच्छायामथिा ज्ञाने जाते वचत्तं वनिेशयेत् ।
आत्मिुद्ध्यानन्यचेतास्ततस्तत्त्वाथधदशधनम् ॥ ९८ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantraṃ
icchāyām athavā jñāne jāte cittaṃ niveśayet |
ātmaśuddhyā ananyacetās tatastattvārthadarśanam || 98 ||
translation: Whether desire or knowledge has arisen, one should place the mind there; through purification of the Self and undivided awareness, then comes the seeing of reality’s meaning.
intent_summary: Use any arising desire or understanding as a single-pointed doorway into purified, nondivided seeing.
beginner_explanation: When a wish or a clear insight appears, don’t scatter your attention. Put your whole mind there and stay with it. If you do this without distraction, the experience can become a doorway to deeper truth.
scholar_explanation: The instruction is to nivēśa citta in icchā or jñāna as they arise, but without division of attention. Through ātmaśuddhi and ananya-cetas, the practitioner gains tattvārtha-darśana, a direct vision of reality beyond fragmented cognition. This verse complements the preceding one by showing that both absence and presence of mental content can be used as supports for recognition.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Seeing Knowledge as Groundless and Relative
sanskrit:
वनवनधवमत्तं भिेज्ज्ञानम् वनराधारं भ्रमात्मकम् ।
तत्त्वत् कस्यवचन्नैतद् एिम्भािी वशि् वप्रये ॥ ९९ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantraṃ
niviśeṣaṃ bhavet jñānaṃ nirādhāraṃ bhramātmakam |
tattvataḥ kasyacid naitad evaṃ bhāvī śivā priye || 99 ||
translation: Knowledge becomes without distinguishing marks, supportless, and made of भ्रम/appearance; in truth it belongs to no one in this way, O beloved of Śiva.
intent_summary: Recognize that ordinary knowledge is unsupported and appearance-like, so it loses its claim to absolute reality.
beginner_explanation: Not every thought or piece of knowledge is solid truth. If you look closely, even certainty can feel like something floating without a real base. Seeing this helps you relax your grip on ideas and rest more deeply.
scholar_explanation: The verse deconstructs jñāna as niviśeṣa and nirādhāra, emphasizing its bhramātmakatva and lack of possessive ownership. This is a subtle nondualist insight: cognition is useful but not ultimately self-grounding, and thus cannot serve as an absolute foundation. The vocative śiva-priye situates the teaching within devotional dialogue while pointing beyond epistemic fixation.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Seeing All Bodies as Made of Consciousness
sanskrit:
वचद्धमाध सिधदेहेषु विशेषो नावस्त कुिवचत् ।
अतश्च तन्मयं सिं भाियन्भिवजज्जन् ॥ १०० ॥
transliteration:
cid dharmāḥ sarvadeheṣu viśeṣo nāsti kutracit |
ataś ca tanmayaṃ sarvaṃ bhāvayan bhajjej janān || 100 ||
translation: The qualities of consciousness are present in all bodies; there is no distinction anywhere. Therefore, by contemplating everything as made of That, one becomes devoted among beings.
intent_summary: Contemplate every body and object as made of consciousness, seeing no real separation anywhere.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that the same awareness is present in every living form. Instead of seeing yourself and others as completely separate, try to feel everything as woven from one living presence. That way, the world becomes less divided and more intimate.
scholar_explanation: The doctrine here is cid-dharma across sarvadeha, denying any ultimate viśeṣa between embodied beings. By bhāvana that all is tanmaya, the practitioner sees the universe as pervaded by consciousness and thereby participates in bhajana as lived recognition rather than external worship. This is a key nondual culmination of the preceding contemplations on desire, knowledge, and groundlessness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Transcending the Defilements
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरि तन्त्रम्
कामक्रोधलोभमोहमदमात्सयधगोचरे ।
िुवद्धं वनवस्तवमतां कृत्वा तत्तत्त्वमिवशष्यते ॥ १०१ ॥
transliteration:
kamakrodhalobhamohamadamātsaryadhagochare |
buddhaṃ nivastamitatāṃ kṛtvā tattattvam aviśiṣyate || 101 ||
translation: In the field of desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, envy, and hatred, establish the intellect in stillness; then that reality remains undivided as the very essence.
intent_summary: The verse teaches the practitioner to become so inwardly steady that even intense afflictive states no longer obscure direct recognition of reality.
beginner_explanation: When strong emotions like anger, greed, or jealousy arise, do not let them pull your attention outward. Let the mind become still instead of fighting with the feeling. In that stillness, the deeper reality behind all these moods can be recognized.
scholar_explanation: This dhāraṇā directs awareness into samatā amid the kāma-krodha-lobha-moha-mada-mātsarya horizon, treating the passions as a field for recognition rather than suppression. By making the buddhi “nivastam” or quietly settled, one abides in tattva as aviśiṣṭa, a non-differentiated reality akin to the nondual Śaiva disclosure of Bhairava-nature. The practical emphasis is not moral purification alone but staying present until the distinction between affect and awareness loosens.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Seeing the World as Illusion
sanskrit:
इन्द्रजालमयं विश्वं व्यस्तं िा वचिकमधित् ।
भ्रमद्वा ध्यायत् सिं पश्यतश्च सुखोद्गम् ॥ १०२ ॥
transliteration:
indrajālamayaṃ viśvaṃ vyastaṃ vā citrakam adhat |
bhramad vā dhyāyat sarvaṃ paśyataś ca sukhodgam || 102 ||
translation: Meditate on the whole universe as made of illusion, or as a scattered picture, or as whirling motion; by seeing everything this way, joy arises.
intent_summary: The verse asks the practitioner to adopt a contemplative vision in which the world is seen as insubstantial, dynamic, and mentally constructed, leading to uplift and ease.
beginner_explanation: Instead of taking the world as fixed and solid, see it like a magic show, a moving painting, or a spinning scene. This changes how much the mind clings to things. That shift can bring a surprising sense of lightness or joy.
scholar_explanation: The instruction uses indrajāla and citra imagery to loosen ordinary realism, presenting viśva as a shimmering display rather than a stable object-world. Such contemplation undermines reification and can open sukhodgama, the spontaneous arising of bliss, because the perceiver sees phenomena as expressive appearances within consciousness. This aligns with the Tantric pedagogy of transforming perception, not rejecting manifestation.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Equanimity Beyond Pleasure and Pain
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरि तन्त्रम्
न वचत्तं वनवक्षपेद् दु्खे न सुखे िा पवरवक्षपेत् ।
भैरवि ज्ञायतां मध्ये वकं तत्त्वमिवशष्यते ॥ १०३ ॥
transliteration:
na cittaṃ nikṣiped duḥkhe na sukhe vā parikṣipet |
bhairavi jñāyatāṃ madhye kiṃ tattvam aviśiṣyate || 103 ||
translation: Do not cast the mind into sorrow, nor throw it into pleasure. O Bhairavī, know what reality remains in the middle.
intent_summary: The verse teaches balanced awareness in the center between pain and pleasure, where the essential nature can be known.
beginner_explanation: Do not get swallowed by bad feelings, and do not get carried away by good ones either. Stay in the middle, watching both come and go. In that calm center, you can notice what remains constant.
scholar_explanation: This dhāraṇā is a direct application of madhya, the central interval, where citta neither collapses into duḥkha nor expands into sukha. The “middle” here is not merely moderation but the liminal gap where dualistic affect fails and the unchanging tattva can disclose itself. It resonates strongly with Śaiva teachings on the interval between opposites as a doorway to recognition.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Seeing the Self Everywhere
sanskrit:
विहाय वनजदेहस्थं सिधिास्मीवत भाियन् ।
दृढेन मनसा दृष्ट्या नान्येवक्षण्या सुखी भिेत् ॥ १०४ ॥
transliteration:
vihāya nijadehasthaṃ sarvatrāsmīti bhāvayan |
dṛḍhena manasā dṛṣṭyā nānyekṣaṇyā sukhī bhavet || 104 ||
translation: Leaving aside the self confined to the body, contemplating, “I am everywhere,” with a firm mind and gaze, one becomes happy by no other way of seeing.
intent_summary: The verse directs the practitioner to expand identity beyond the body and rest in all-pervading selfhood.
beginner_explanation: Try not to feel trapped inside your body like you are only a small person inside skin. Instead, sense “I am everywhere” and hold that feeling steadily. Seeing this way can bring a deep happiness that does not depend on outside things.
scholar_explanation: The practice negates nijadeha-stha identification and replaces it with sarvatrāsmīti-bhāvanā, an expansion of selfhood into universal presence. This is not imagination in a merely psychological sense but a yogic reorientation toward vyāpti, the all-pervading nature of consciousness. The “dṛḍha” mind and sight stabilize the intuition until alternative modes of perception lose force.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Recognizing Consciousness in All Things
sanskrit:
घटादौ यच्च विज्ञानवमच्छाद्यं िा ममान्तरे ।
नैि सिधगतं जातं भाियवन्नवत सिधग् ॥ १०५ ॥
transliteration:
ghaṭādau yac ca vijñānam icchādyaṃ vā mamāntare |
naiva sarvagataṃ jātaṃ bhāvayan niśi sarvag || 105 ||
translation: Whatever consciousness is in a pot and the like, or within desire and other states in me—meditating thus, it has never truly become all-pervading; it is ever-present.
intent_summary: The verse teaches recognition of consciousness as already present in objects, inner states, and every circumstance, rather than as something newly produced.
beginner_explanation: Notice the same awareness in a pot, in a feeling, and in your own mind. Do not think consciousness only appears at certain times or places. It is already there everywhere, like space in every room.
scholar_explanation: This dhāraṇā points to vijñāna as inherent in ghatādi and in icchādi internal states, negating the notion that consciousness is a newly arisen product. The wording suggests an omnipresent awareness that is not limited by the specific form it illumines, fitting Śaiva nondualism’s claim that consciousness is the substrate of all manifestations. The practice is contemplative recognition of prior presence rather than meditative construction.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Maintaining Awareness of Subject and Object
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
ग्राह्यग्राहकसवित्त्वं सामान्या सिद्धदेवधनानाम् ।
योगिनां तु विशेषोऽस्ति सम्बन्धे सािधानता ॥ १०६ ॥
transliteration:
grāhyagrāhakasattvaṃ sāmānyaṃ siddhadevatāhnām |
yogināṃ tu viśeṣo'sti sambandhe sādhānatā || 106 ||
translation: The common nature of the accomplished gods is the reality of grasped and grasper; for yogins there is a special distinction: careful attention to relationship.
intent_summary: The verse teaches refined awareness of the relation between subject and object, using it as a yogic key rather than as a source of bondage.
beginner_explanation: Usually we feel like a separate person looking at separate things. This verse says that wise beings understand that the connection between observer and observed is important. By paying close attention to that connection, meditation deepens.
scholar_explanation: The verse distinguishes the sādhana of yogins from the more ordinary siddhadeva condition by emphasizing grāhya-grāhaka-sattva and sambandha-sādhānatā. Rather than collapsing subject and object prematurely, the yogin observes the dynamic relation until it is seen as a mode of awareness itself. This relational attentiveness can serve as a bridge into nondual recognition.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Expanding into Another’s Body
sanskrit:
स्विदन्यशरीरेऽपि सवित्त्वं अनुभावयेत् ।
अपेक्षां स्वशरीरस्य त्यक्त्वा व्यापी भवेत् ॥ १०७ ॥
transliteration:
svadanyasharīre'pi sattvaṃ anubhāvayet |
apekṣāṃ svaśarīrasya tyaktvā vyāpī bhavet || 107 ||
translation: One should experience consciousness even in another’s body; abandoning concern for one’s own body, one becomes all-pervading.
intent_summary: The verse trains the practitioner to loosen bodily self-boundaries and feel consciousness as present beyond this one body.
beginner_explanation: Try to sense awareness not as trapped inside your own body alone. Imagine that consciousness is also present in others. As you stop clinging to “my body,” the feeling of being limited can open out.
scholar_explanation: This practice extends sattva-anubhava beyond svaśarīra, producing a sense of vyāpti and de-centering possessive bodily identity. It is a nondual exercise in loosening ahamkāra’s bodily enclosure by recognizing consciousness in others as one’s own luminous nature. The verse also implicitly supports compassion, because other bodies are no longer fundamentally “other” in the field of awareness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Resting in the Nondual Self
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरि तन्त्रम्
वनराधारं मन् कृत्वा विकल्पान्न विकल्पयेत् ।
तदात्मपरमात्मत्वे भैरिो मृगलोचने ॥ १०८ ॥
transliteration:
nirādhāraṃ manaḥ kṛtvā vikalpān na vikalpayet |
tadātmaparamātmatve bhairavo mṛgalocane || 108 ||
translation: Making the mind supportless, do not generate thoughts from thoughts. O deer-eyed one, then Bhairava is the identity of the individual self and the supreme Self.
intent_summary: The verse teaches letting the mind become free of supports and conceptual proliferation so nondual identity can be directly known.
beginner_explanation: Let the mind stand without leaning on any idea, memory, or story. When thoughts stop feeding more thoughts, the sense of being a small separate self can soften. Then you may directly feel that the deep self and the highest self are one.
scholar_explanation: Nirādhāra-manas is the collapse of conceptual scaffolding, and the injunction not to vikalpa from vikalpa interrupts the self-reinforcing chain of mental construction. The revelation is tad-ātmā-paramātmatva, a classical Śaiva nondual identity of jīva and Śiva/Bhairava. This is a quintessential recognition teaching: not fabrication, but the unveiling of what is already the case.

speaker: Bhairava
title: I Am the Supreme Lord
sanskrit:
सिधज्ञ् सिधकताध च व्यापक् परमेश्वर् ।
स एिाहम् शैिधमाध इवत दार्ढ्ाधवच्छिो भिेत् ॥ १०९ ॥
transliteration:
siddhajñaṃ siddhakartrā ca vyāpakaṃ parameśvaram |
sa evāhaṃ śaivamāheti iti dārḍhyād avacchinnaḥ bhavet || 109 ||
translation: The accomplished knower, the accomplished doer, the all-pervading Supreme Lord—firmly established in the thought, “That alone am I, this is the Śaiva Great,” one becomes undivided.
intent_summary: The verse teaches firm conviction in one’s identity with the all-pervading Supreme Lord, dissolving limiting self-concepts.
beginner_explanation: Repeat inwardly that the highest reality is not separate from you: the knower, the doer, the all-pervading Lord. Hold this not as a slogan but as a steady inner certainty. Over time, that certainty can loosen the feeling of being small and divided.
scholar_explanation: The verse uses dārḍhya, firmness, to stabilize the recognition that siddhajña, siddhakartṛ, and vyāpaka parameśvara are not distinct realities from oneself. The phrase sa evāham articulates a direct nondual identification characteristic of Śaiva self-recognition, while avacchinna suggests that limitation is what is to be overcome. This is less an inference than an affirmative contemplative fixing of identity.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Wave-Like Forms of the World
sanskrit:
जलस्येिोमधयो िह्नेर्ज्ाधलाभङ्ग्य् प्रभा रिे् ।
ममैि भैरिस्यैता विश्वभङ्ग्यो विभेवदता् ॥ ११० ॥
transliteration:
jalasyevormayo vahner jvālābhaṅgyaḥ prabhā raveḥ |
mamaiva bhairavasyaitā viśvabhaṅgyo vibhedataḥ || 110 ||
translation: As waves are of water, as flames are the play of fire, as rays are the radiance of the sun, so these forms of the universe are distinctions of me, Bhairava.
intent_summary: The verse teaches seeing all world-forms as expressions of Bhairava, like waves from water or rays from the sun.
beginner_explanation: Think of the world like waves arising from the ocean. The waves look separate, but they are never apart from water. In the same way, all the changing forms of life are expressions of one deeper reality.
scholar_explanation: This is a classic analogy of manifestation as non-separable expression: viśvabhaṅgī are differentiated appearances within Bhairava, just as waves, flames, and rays are not other than their substrates. The verse supports a bheda-as-abheda reading in which difference is acknowledged phenomenally but denied ultimate independence. It is a powerful contemplative image for integrating multiplicity into nondual vision.

speaker: Bhairava
title: From Agitation to the Supreme State
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
भ्रान्त्वा भ्रान्त्वा शरीरेण त्ववरतम् भुवि पातनात् ।
क्षोभशविविरामेण परा संजायते दशा ॥ १११ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantram |
bhrāntvā bhrāntvā śarīreṇa tvavaratam bhuvi pātanāt |
kṣobhaśavivirāmeṇa parā saṃjāyate daśā || 111 ||
translation: Having wandered again and again with the body, and by repeatedly falling to the ground, when agitation and exhaustion come to rest, the supreme state arises.
intent_summary: Use bodily exhaustion and the settling of agitation as a doorway into a higher contemplative state.
beginner_explanation: This verse points to a surprising idea: after intense physical movement and total fatigue, the mind can suddenly become quiet. When the body can no longer keep up its restlessness, a deeper stillness may appear on its own. The practice is not to force anything, but to notice the pause after effort.
scholar_explanation: This dhāraṇā uses repeated bodily motion and subsequent kṣobha-śavi-virāma, the cessation of agitation, as a trigger for parā-dāśā. It belongs to the VBT’s strategy of using extremity and collapse of ordinary activity to reveal the ever-present ground of consciousness. The emphasis is not on ascetic suffering itself, but on the moment when effort exhausts vikalpa and the nondual state becomes manifest.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Bhairava Revealed at the End of Agitation
sanskrit:
आधारेष्वथिाऽशक्त्याऽज्ञानावच्चित्तलयेन िा ।
जातशविसमावेशक्षोभान्ते भैरिं िपु् ॥ ११२ ॥
transliteration:
ādhāreṣvathāśaktyājñānāvac cittalayena vā |
jātaśaktisamāveśakṣobhānte bhairavaṃ vapuḥ || 112 ||
translation: Or, in the supports, when there is incapacity and ignorance, or by the dissolution of mind, at the end of the agitation of the arising of power, the body becomes Bhairava.
intent_summary: See the body itself as Bhairava when mental activity collapses and power subsides into direct presence.
beginner_explanation: Here the teaching is that when the mind stops chattering and your usual sense of control weakens, the body can be experienced differently. Instead of feeling like a solid thing that belongs to you, it may be seen as pure presence. The verse invites you to notice that even the body can reveal a deeper awareness.
scholar_explanation: The verse points to ādhāra-based contemplation in which aśakti and ajñāna, or alternatively cittalaya, culminate in śakti-samāveśa-kṣobhānta. At that threshold, the deha is recognized as bhairavam vapuḥ, not as inert matter but as the vibratory manifestation of consciousness. This aligns with Trika’s view that embodied experience is never outside Cit/Śakti, only misrecognized through contraction.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Still Gazing into the Eyes
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
सम्प्रदायवममं देवि शृणु सम्यविदाम्यहम् ।
कैवल्यं जायते सद्यो नेत्रयोः स्तब्धमात्रयोः ॥ ११३ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantram |
sampradāyam imaṃ devi śṛṇu samyag vadiāmyaham |
kaivalyaṃ jāyate sadyo netrayoḥ stabdhamātrayoḥ || 113 ||
translation: Devi, listen well to this tradition I am telling you: liberation (kaivalya) arises immediately when the eyes become perfectly still.
intent_summary: Hold the gaze motionless so that ordinary mental movement falls away and liberation can appear.
beginner_explanation: This practice uses the eyes. Instead of looking around, you keep your gaze steady and still. As the eyes become quiet, the mind can also become quiet, like water settling when it is no longer stirred.
scholar_explanation: Bhairava presents an ācāra or sampradāya specifically tied to netra-stabdhatā. The stillness of the eyes interrupts outward projection (bāhya-vṛtti) and allows kaivalya to flash forth immediately, indicating that liberation is not produced but disclosed. This is a classic VBT visual-attentional dhāraṇā, related to tractable gazing practices and the arrest of discursive movement.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Closing the Ears and Lower Gates
sanskrit:
सम्कोचं कर्णयोः कृत्वा ह्यधोद्वारे तथैव च ।
अनच्कमहलं ध्यायविशेद्ब्रह्म सनातनम् ॥ ११४ ॥
transliteration:
saṃko caṃ karṇayoḥ kṛtvā hyadhodvāre tathaiva ca |
anacakam ahalaṃ dhyāyed brahma sanātanam || 114 ||
translation: Having closed the ears, and likewise the lower gate, one should meditate on the imperishable house, the eternal Brahman.
intent_summary: Withdraw the senses and attention inward to rest in the imperishable reality.
beginner_explanation: This verse recommends shutting out incoming distractions and turning attention away from the lower bodily openings. With the senses quieted, you focus on what is stable and unchanging. It is like closing doors so you can rest in a silent room.
scholar_explanation: The instruction combines karṇa-saṃkoca and ādhodvāra-saṃkoca with dhyāna on the anacakam ahalam, the imperishable inner abode. The text suggests a sensory withdrawal that supports access to sanātana brahman, though within VBT this is the lived recognition of one's own imperishable consciousness rather than an external theism. The verse echoes pratyāhāra while retaining the Tantric aim of immediate realization.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Looking Down into the Well-Space
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरि तन्त्रम्
कूपावदके महागते वस्थित्वोपरि निरीक्षणात् ।
अविकल्पमते् सम्यक्सद्यवश्चत्तलय् िुटम् ॥ ११५ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantram |
kūpāvadake mahāgate viṣṭhityopari nirīkṣaṇāt |
avikalpamateḥ samyak sadyas cittalayam bhavet || 115 ||
translation: By standing above a great opening like a well and looking down, with a mind free of conceptualization, the mind is dissolved immediately.
intent_summary: Use a vast downward opening to trigger nonconceptual absorption and mental dissolution.
beginner_explanation: Here the instruction is to look into a deep open space, like a well, while keeping the mind free of thought. The feeling of depth can help the mind let go of its usual grip. It is a way of using space itself to quiet the inner commentary.
scholar_explanation: This dhāraṇā uses vertical depth-perception—kūpa-like openness—as an external support for avikalpa. The upward stance with downward gaze produces a perceptual vertigo that dissolves conceptual fixation and leads to cittalaya. In Trika terms, the external void becomes a mirror for the inner viśrānti into awareness free of vikalpa.

speaker: Bhairava
title: The Everywhere of Consciousness
sanskrit:
यि यि मनो यावत िाह्ये िाभ्यन्तरेऽवप िा ।
ति ति वशिािास्था व्यापकत्वात्क्व यास्यवत ॥ ११६ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantram |
yatra yatra mano yātv bāhye vābhyantare'pi vā |
tatra tatra śivāvāsthā vyāpakatvātkva yāsyati || 116 ||
translation: Wherever the mind goes, outside or even inside, there the condition of Śiva abides; because of its all-pervading nature, where could it go?
intent_summary: Recognize that every perceived place is already permeated by Śiva, so no experience is outside the divine presence.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that no matter where your mind wanders—outward, inward, anywhere—Śiva is already there. That means you do not need to chase a special location to find awareness. The search itself relaxes when you realize there is nowhere else to go.
scholar_explanation: The verse articulates vyāptitva: Śiva as all-pervasive presence in every domain of mental movement, bāhya and abhyantara alike. Since every locus of mind is already within śivāvasthā, spatialized seeking is exposed as unnecessary. The teaching strongly affirms nonlocality of consciousness and functions as a corrective to projection and spiritual dualism.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Mind Dissolves in Any Sense Gate
sanskrit:
यि यिाक्षमागेण चैतन्यं व्यज्यते विभो् ।
तस्य तन्मािधवमधत्वावच्चल्लयाद्भवरतात्मता ॥ ११७ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantram |
yatra yatra'kṣamārgeṇa caitanyaṃ vyajyate vibhoḥ |
tasya tanmātradharmitvāc callayād bhairavātmatā || 117 ||
translation: Wherever consciousness is manifested through a sense-door, because of its nature as a subtle object (tanmātra), through its movement one attains Bhairava-nature.
intent_summary: Use any sensory entry point as a gateway for consciousness to dissolve into Bhairava-identity.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that any sense experience can become a doorway. When you notice seeing, hearing, or touching very closely, the usual sense of separation can soften. Then the experience can open into a deeper feeling of being one with everything.
scholar_explanation: Here caitanya appears through any akṣamārga, and by attending to its tanmātra-dharma and movement (cala) one enters bhairavātmatā. The verse reflects the VBT method of treating sensory processes not as obstacles but as apertures into the nature of consciousness. The subtle-object aspect is important: one follows sensation to the threshold where subject-object structure collapses.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Turning Crisis into Brahmic Presence
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
क्षुताद्यन्ते भये शोके गह्वरे वा रणाद्द्रुते ।
कुतूहलेक्षुधाद्यन्ते ब्रह्मसत्तामयी दशा ॥ ११८ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantram |
khṣutādyante bhaye śoke gahvare vā raṇāddrutae |
kutūhule kṣudhādyante brahmasattāmayī daśā || 118 ||
translation: At the end of hunger and such states, in fear, sorrow, in a cavern, or when fleeing from battle, at the height of curiosity, at the end of hunger and the like, there is a state made of Brahman’s reality.
intent_summary: Transform intense affective states into immediate access to a Brahman-like mode of being.
beginner_explanation: Strong feelings like fear, grief, hunger, or even intense curiosity can shake up the mind. This verse says those moments can also open a deeper state if you stay present with them. Instead of running from the feeling, you let it reveal a more spacious awareness.
scholar_explanation: The verse names liminal affective conditions—bhaya, śoka, kṣut, and kutūhala—as catalysts for brahma-sattā-mayī daśā. These intense states suspend ordinary self-construction and can reveal a more immediate ontological texture of consciousness. The teaching is consistent with the VBT’s use of extremes as soteriological openings rather than mere disturbances.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Let the Body Float without Support
sanskrit:
वस्तुषु स्मयधमाणेषु दृष्टे देशे मनस् त्यजेत् ।
स्वशरीरं निराधारं कृत्वा प्रसरवत् प्रभुः ॥ ११९ ॥
transliteration:
vastuṣu smaryamāṇeṣu dṛṣṭe deśe manas tyajet |
svaśarīraṃ nirādhāraṃ kṛtvā prasarat prabhuḥ || 119 ||
translation: When objects are being remembered, in a seen place, one should let go of the mind; having made one's own body supportless, the Lord extends forth.
intent_summary: Release attention from objects and feel the body as weightless, allowing expansive presence to emerge.
beginner_explanation: This practice tells you to stop clinging to whatever you are thinking about or seeing. Then imagine your body as if it had no support, like it were floating or spreading out. That can help you feel less cramped inside your usual sense of self.
scholar_explanation: By withdrawing manas from remembered objects in the dr̥ṣṭa-deśa, one makes the svaśarīra nirādhāra. The result is prasarat prabhuḥ, the expansive unfolding of lordly consciousness beyond bodily contraction. This verse bridges sensory de-centering and nondual embodiment, closely allied with dhāraṇās on spaciousness and all-pervasive awareness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Object-Filled Mind Becomes a Void Abode
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
क्ववचद्वस्तुवन विन्यस्य शनैदृधवष्टम् वनितधयेत् ।
तज्ज्ञानं वचत्तसवहतं देवि शून्यालयो भिेत् ॥१२० ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantram |
kvacid vastuni vinyasya śanai dṛḍham uccārya vanitadhayet |
tajjñānaṃ cittasahitaṃ devi śūnyālayo bhavet || 120 ||
translation: Fixing the mind on some object somewhere and then slowly and firmly contemplating it, O Devi, that knowledge together with the mind becomes a dwelling in the void.
intent_summary: Use steady contemplation of an object until the mind and knowing settle into emptiness.
beginner_explanation: Choose one thing and hold it in attention very steadily, without rushing. As your attention becomes simple and unmixed, the mind can become quiet and open. Then even the act of knowing feels spacious, almost empty.
scholar_explanation: The dhāraṇā prescribes deliberate fixation on a vastu followed by dṛḍha, slow contemplation until taj-jñāna with citta becomes śūnyālaya. Rather than seeking an external void, the practice reveals that cognition itself can rest as empty abode when conceptual proliferation subsides. This is a classic VBT strategy: concentration on form leading to formlessness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Devotional Intensity as Shakti
sanskrit:
भक्त्युद्रेकावद्वरिस्य यादृशी जायते मवत् ।
सा शवि् शाङ्करी वनत्यं भियेत्तां तत् वशि् ॥ १२१ ॥
transliteration:
bhaktyudrekāvadvarisya yādṛśī jāyate mavat |
 sā śaviḥ śāṅkarī vanatyaṃ bhiyettāṃ tat vaśiḥ || 121 ||
translation: Whatever state arises through an outpouring of devotion—such is the Shakti of Śaṅkara. Continually abiding in that, one becomes absorbed in it.
intent_summary: Use heightened devotion as a force that carries the mind into absorption in the divine power of Śiva.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that when devotion becomes very strong, it naturally transforms your state of mind. Instead of forcing concentration, you let love for the divine intensify until it carries you inward. The practice is to stay with that devotional feeling until it becomes steady and absorbing.
scholar_explanation: Bhakti-udreka here functions as an upāya: the rising of devotion itself reveals śakti, specifically śāṅkarī-śakti. In Kashmir Śaivism, intense affect can become a direct gateway into awareness when not held as an object but allowed to saturate the subject. The practitioner abides in that force until vaśitā or mastery/entrancement occurs.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Emptying into the Gaps
sanskrit:
िस्त्वन्तरे िेद्यमाने सिधिस्तुषु शून्यता ।
तामेि मनसा ध्यात्वा विवदतोऽवप प्रशाम्यवत ॥ १२२ ॥
transliteration:
istvantare vedyamāne sidhistuṣu śūnyatā |
 tāmeva manasā dhyātvā vidadito'pi praśāmyati || 122 ||
translation: When the intervals between states are perceived, there is emptiness. Meditating with the mind on that very emptiness, even the disturbed one becomes pacified.
intent_summary: Notice the gaps between mental events and rest attention there until agitation subsides.
beginner_explanation: Between thoughts, breaths, and moods there is a small gap. This verse tells you to notice that gap and simply rest in it. Even if your mind is restless, repeatedly returning to that openness helps calm it.
scholar_explanation: The dhāraṇā points to śūnyatā as the felt interval between saṃvid-events, often correlated with the transitions among waking, dream, deep sleep, or between cognitive acts. By dhyāna on that gap, the practitioner tastes a nonconceptual stillness that pacifies even a vikṣipta mind. This is a classic laya-oriented approach through the pause or in-between (madhya).

speaker: Bhairava
title: Beyond Purity and Impurity
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरि तन्त्रम्
वकंवचज्ज्ञैयाध स्मृता शुवद्ध् सा शुवद्ध् शम्भुदशधने ।
न शुवचह्यधशुवचस्तस्मावन्नविधकल्प् सुखी भिेत् ॥ १२३ ॥
transliteration:
vijñāna-bhairava tantraṃ
kiṃcidjñeyādhā smṛtā śuddhiḥ sā śuddhiḥ śambhudarśane |
 na śucirhy-aśucis tasmānna vikalpaḥ sukhaṃ bhavet || 123 ||
translation: Knowledge of a certain thing is remembered as purity; that purity is in the vision of Śambhu. For in reality there is neither pure nor impure, so by the absence of विकल्प (mental construction) one becomes सुखी, happy.
intent_summary: Let go of judging experience as pure or impure and rest in undivided awareness beyond conceptual distinctions.
beginner_explanation: We usually label things as clean or dirty, good or bad, acceptable or not. This verse says that in the deepest view of consciousness, those labels are mental constructions. If you stop dividing experience that way, a natural ease appears.
scholar_explanation: The verse undermines ritual and conceptual bifurcation by locating śuddhi in śambhu-darśana, not in external classification. The key is nirvikalpa, freedom from vikalpa, where the duality of śuci/aśuci collapses in nondual awareness. This reflects the Trika tendency to relocate purity into recognition (pratyabhijñā) rather than convention.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Seeing Bhairava Everywhere
sanskrit:
सिधि भैरिो भाि् सामान्येष्ववप गोचर् ।
न च तद्व्यवतरेिेण परोऽस्तीत्यद्वया गवत् ॥ १२४ ॥
transliteration:
sarvaṃ bhairavo bhāvaḥ sāmānyeṣvapi gocaraḥ |
 na ca tadvyatirekeṇa paro'stītyadvayā gatiḥ || 124 ||
translation: Everything is Bhairava; his nature is accessible even in ordinary things. Apart from that, there is nothing else—this is the movement of nonduality.
intent_summary: Perceive every ordinary perception as Bhairava and abandon the idea of a separate reality outside him.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that the divine is not only in special spiritual experiences. It is present in ordinary sights, sounds, and events too. Practice means learning to see the same sacred reality in everything, without imagining a separate world outside it.
scholar_explanation: Here Bhairava is sarvaṃ and also common (sāmānya), indicating that the absolute is not confined to extraordinary states. The statement that nothing exists apart from that is a concise formulation of advaya-gati, the nondual path of recognition. This verse bridges ontological doctrine and contemplative perception.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Equanimity in Honor and Dishonor
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
सम् शिौ च वमिे च समो मानािमानयो् ॥
ब्रह्मण् पवरपूणधत्वावदवत ज्ञात्वा सुखी भिेत् ॥ १२५ ॥
transliteration:
vijñāna-bhairava tantraṃ
samaṃ śatrau ca mitre ca samo mānāvamānayoḥ ||
 brahmaṇaḥ paripūrṇatvāditi jñātvā sukhī bhavet || 125 ||
translation: Equal toward enemy and friend, equal toward honor and dishonor—knowing this from the पूर्णता (wholeness) of Brahman, one becomes happy.
intent_summary: Cultivate equal awareness amid opposites by recognizing the fullness of Brahman in all circumstances.
beginner_explanation: This verse teaches steadiness. Whether someone praises you or criticizes you, likes you or opposes you, try to stay balanced inside. When you stop riding the waves of approval and rejection, you feel more free and peaceful.
scholar_explanation: The sādhana is sāmya, equal vision toward śatru/mitra and māna/avamāna, grounded in brahmaṇaḥ paripūrṇatva, the fullness of the absolute. This is not emotional repression but an awakened equanimity that arises from recognizing completeness in consciousness itself. It resonates with Trika notions of svātantrya and unaffectedness amid relational polarities.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Transcending Attraction and Aversion
sanskrit:
न द्वेषं भाियेत्क्वावप न रागं भाियेत्क्ववचत् ।
रागद्वेषविवनमुधिौ मध्ये ब्रह्म प्रसपधवत ॥ १२६ ॥
transliteration:
na dveṣaṃ bhāvayेत्क्वāpi na rāgaṃ bhāvayetkvacit |
 rāgadveṣavininirmuktau madhye brahma prasarpati || 126 ||
translation: One should not foster hatred anywhere, nor foster attachment anywhere. When free from attachment and hatred, Brahman spreads through the middle.
intent_summary: Release both attraction and aversion so the middle openness of Brahman can reveal itself.
beginner_explanation: The mind gets trapped by what it likes and dislikes. This verse says not to feed either side. When you stop chasing what you want and pushing away what you fear, something wider and calmer can shine through.
scholar_explanation: Rāga and dveṣa are the classic affective pair binding the jīva to dualistic movement. Their cessation does not mean indifference in a negative sense, but entry into the madhya, the central flow where brahma-prasaraṇa occurs. This resembles the Trika emphasis on the middle interval as a site of unconditioned awareness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Universalizing Bhairava
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
यदिेद्यं यदग्राह्यं यच्छून्यं यदभािगम् ।
तत्सिं भैरिं भाव्यं तदन्ते िोधसम्भि् ॥ १२७ ॥
transliteration:
vijñāna-bhairava tantraṃ
yadvedyaṃ yadagrāhyaṃ yacchūnyaṃ yadabhāvagam |
 tatsarvaṃ bhairavaṃ bhāvyaṃ tadante bodhasambhavaḥ || 127 ||
translation: Whatever is knowable, whatever is ungraspable, whatever is empty, whatever is beyond being: all that should be contemplated as Bhairava; at the end, awakening arises.
intent_summary: Contemplate every mode of experience and even what lies beyond grasping as Bhairava until awareness dawns.
beginner_explanation: This verse tells you to include everything in your meditation—not just pleasant or clear experiences, but also the unknown, the empty, and what you cannot hold onto. Instead of excluding anything, see it all as one sacred presence. That inclusive view can lead to a breakthrough in understanding.
scholar_explanation: The verse expands bhāvanā to all phenomenological registers: vedya, agrāhya, śūnya, and abhāvagam, thereby eliminating any remainder outside Bhairava. The result is bodha-sambhava, the arising of luminous knowing, consistent with the nondual totality of the Trika worldview. It is a radical universalization of contemplative identity.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Immersing in Inner Space
sanskrit:
वनत्ये वनराश्रये शून्ये व्यापके कलनोविते ।
िाह्याकाशे मनः कृत्वा वनराकाशं समाविशेत् ॥ १२८ ॥
transliteration:
nitye nirāśraye śūnye vyāpake kalanocite |
 bāhyākāśe manaḥ kṛtvā nirākāśaṃ samāviśet || 128 ||
translation: In the eternal, unsupported, empty, all-pervading, and subtle expanse, placing the mind in external space, one should enter the spaceless.
intent_summary: Use attention on outer space or vastness to move beyond spatial form into the boundless inner expanse.
